Exactly how much Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) headroom do Manchester United have to back Mauricio Pochettino in the January transfer window?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino has barely unpacked his bags at Old Trafford, but it's already abundantly clear Manchester United need to back their new head coach in January.

Following a disappointing start to the campaign and the arrival of a new regulatory era in English football, the club’s latest financial results offer a clear picture as to how much room INEOS actually have to manoeuvre.

Man United’s most recent full-year accounts, covering the 12-month period to 30 June, 2026, which were published in September, paints a picture of cost-cutting paired with historically strong commercial standing.

Despite having no European football last season, Man United posted record revenue of £677.6 million while trimming wages for a third consecutive year to £302.0m.

Although previous recruitment pushed player amortisation to £211.8m and left a net loss of £43.0m after finance costs, £47.0m in player-sale profits kept the underlying business moving forward.

Even more telling are Man United’s first-quarter results for 2026/27, released on November 19.

With Champions League football back at Old Trafford, quarterly revenue rose 4.1 per cent to £146.1m, and the club are predicted to earn £740m and £760m annually.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Quarterly player amortisation fell by almost 15 per cent following summer exits and Casemiro’s contract expiry, while another £20.7m was banked in player-disposal profits.

This summer, the Premier League replaced Profitability and Sustainability Rules (PSR) with its new Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) system. Under SCR, clubs’ on-pitch spending - which comprises first-team player and head coach wages, transfer amortisation, and agent fees, while excluding non-playing staff, academy and women’s team costs - is capped at 85 per cent of football revenue plus net profit on player sales.

There is even a 30 per cent multi-year buffer up to a 115 per cent ‘Red Threshold’ before points deductions apply. However, because Man United are competing in the Champions League, they must simultaneously adhere to UEFA’s stricter 70 per cent squad cost limit ahead of the March 1 compliance checkpoint.

Therefore, Pochettino has far more breathing room in the transfer market than naysayers might suggest.

Taking the £750m midpoint of Man United’s expected 2026/27 revenue and adding roughly £45m - which is an average of player-trading profits over recent years - that gives an adjusted revenue figure of £795m.

Under the Premier League’s 85 per cent threshold, Man United could carry £675.8m in annual squad costs. Under UEFA’s tighter 70 per cent ceiling, their limit sits at £556.5m.

Remove non-playing staff from total wages and Man United’s first-team player and coaching bill sits near £255m. Add £186.4m in annualised amortisation and roughly £35m in agents’ fees, and total squad costs land around £476.4m - roughly 60 per cent of adjusted revenue.

That leaves roughly £80m in annual squad-cost headroom beneath UEFA’s 70 per cent cap - and nearly £200m domestically.

This means Man United could comfortably sanction £120m to £150m in winter transfer spending. That said, their borrowing position and existing credit facility could yet prove to be a handbrake on any January rebuild, but from a purely regulatory standpoint, Man United's transfer expenditure picture is a rosy one.

#897. London’s people-first approach to smart-city development

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Benjamin Plackett is a science journalist based in London.

A virtual-reality model of London’s main financial district, the City of London, has mapped the size and location of every building.Credit: Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images

London has risen to fourth place in the IMD Smart City Index 2026, up from sixth place in 2025 and eighth place in 2024. The index — which is published by IMD, an independent Swiss business institute — draws mostly on residents’ perceptions of infrastructure and technology, not a tally of sensors. That focus on perspective is important, says Trevor Dorling, managing director of DG Cities, a private urban-innovation consultancy spun out of the Royal Borough of Greenwich local authority, which works to make better use of data and introduce new technologies in the southeast London borough.

“We increasingly describe our work as ‘city innovation’ rather than ‘smart cities’, because in many people’s minds ‘smart’ is associated with gadgets and gizmos,” says Dorling. “The aim is to use technology to create better places for people. It shouldn’t be the technologists who define what ‘better’ is, but the communities that live there.”

There is plenty of evidence that London has the resources and knowledge to apply research solutions in such a people-centred way. In the 2026 Nature Index Science Cities table, London is ranked 21st overall, but it jumps to 5th place for health-sciences output, for instance.

The Smart Mobility Living Lab, created by a consortium of public and private organizations, including DG Cities, spans 24 kilometres of roads in Greenwich and the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford, and is one example of London’s efforts to create societal impact with its innovation.

The area has more than 1,000 different road features, from speed bumps and pedestrian crossings to one-way systems and bridges, that allow companies to test new vehicles and services in busy, real-world complexity. “The driving force for this was the rapid development of self-driving technologies and exploring the opportunities this presented for safety and accessibility, as well as the challenges,” says Dorling.

Trials to test self-driving shuttle buses and delivery vans have put the technology in public view, with residents invited to ride in the test vehicles, an openness that Dorling says has helped overcome scepticism and brought local authorities into the development process at an early stage.

London’s digital-twin projects are similarly pragmatic. The local authority in Harrow (northwest London) uses high-resolution drone imagery to inspect and measure roofs and buildings remotely and to build interactive maps of parks. The council used this approach in April 2026 to make a 3D model of Headstone Manor and Museum — a restored medieval complex and local-history museum — saving £12,000 (US$16,260) by avoiding a conventional roof survey with scaffolding and manual inspections.

In London’s main financial district, known as the City of London, a virtual-reality model created by the local authority in collaboration with researchers and digital spatial mappers has captured the size and location of every building, window, lamppost and traffic light within the area to within two centimetres of accuracy, allowing planners and the public to properly scrutinize building proposals.

Elsa Arcaute, a complexity science researcher at University College London, cautions against too much faith in digital twins, as a city with all its complexity and interplay between urbanity, nature and human behaviour cannot be completely duplicated.

#896. Erling Haaland brands Man City ‘not good enough’ after Napoli draw

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

City have won just one of their last seven games in all competitions

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Erling Haaland stated that Manchester City were "not good enough" after snatching a 2-2 Champions League draw against Napoli at home.

Rayan Cherki struck in the 86th-minute to equalise, allowing City to come from behind a second time and avoid defeat against the Italians on Tuesday.

The outcome prolongs a frustrating spell of form for City, who have secured victory in just one of their last seven matches across all competitions.

The City striker told TNT Sports: “We tried to push at the end for a goal but we couldn’t – not good enough and we let them in too easily.

“We were not able to control and attack the game in the way we want.

“Football is easy and difficult – when you win it’s easy and you know what to do. When you don’t, you start questioning everything.

“The perfect thing would be to not think but it’s not so easy.

“We have so much quality so it’s about getting the quality out in every player.

“We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.”

After a tame first half, City fell behind to a goal from former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund after 55 minutes.

Ayyoub Bouaddi pulled them back into the game but City needed to fight back again after Noa Lang restored Napoli’s lead with a fine volley 14 minutes from time.

Cherki’s leveller was a fine individual effort but the Frenchman felt the overall performance had been a flat one.

He said: “I don’t care about scoring, I just want to win. We played good but we didn’t play with energy, we need to do more.

“Today was like the last games, we need to work more.”

City manager Enzo Maresca laughed when told of Cherki’s comments, insisting there were positives to build on.

The Italian said: “No, I think tonight we pressed very aggressive, we recovered the ball most of the time. Off the ball I think the team was good, from my point of view.

“We created a lot of chances but it was difficult. We expected Napoli to play a waiting game in a low block.

“We conceded few chances, and the goals we conceded could have been avoided.

“There is a degree of regret we didn’t win but when you can’t win, don’t lose. We take the point and go forward.”

#895. Emery unhappy with ‘unfair’ referee but Aston Villa are toothless

Six months after the glory of that Europa League final, Aston Villa’s return to Istanbul proved a chastening night of disappointment.

Unai Emery’s team have undergone a significant rebuild since that stirring night in May and this was another occasion where Villa 2.0 were exposed as a work in progress.

Emery’s run without a win has extended to six matches in all competitions and Villa’s Champions League campaign does not promise to get any easier, with Paris St-Germain up next.

There was always likely to be a period of transition this season, as six of the heroes from the Europa League final’s starting XI were sold over the summer.

Despite some encouraging signs before the last international break, and three successive Champions League wins, Villa are now enduring a difficult run.

Their second-half performance in particular was poor, and Galatasaray secured victory with the evening’s first shot on target.

The deadlock is FINALLY broken 🙌 Deniz Gül gives Galatasaray the lead after a scramble in front of the net. 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SplkgZC63p

Emery was booked late on as his frustrations got the better of him. His team appear short of creativity and, when Nicolas Jackson struggles, are toothless in the final third.

Though Villa did frustrate the Turkish champions for long periods on a slow, substandard pitch, this was a second successive defeat in the Champions League. Emery now faces a daunting double-header against PSG and Borussia Dortmund. They may still have enough to qualify for the knockout stages, but Villa fans of a certain vintage will insist their team never do it the easy way.

Emery was unhappy with the performance of German referee Daniel Siebert and said: “I am disappointed a little bit. After their goal, it was impossible to play. They wasted time. They added only five minutes. OK, finish the match. We don’t want to play more, I don’t think the referee was fair there. Two years ago we lost to Brugge and Monaco away [in the Champions League]. Today I can compare this match to those matches.”

Alejandro Garnacho, the Chelsea loanee, did not travel and was absent from the match-day squad for the fourth game in a row. Emery said: “Today the players were here who I think are the best players to be here with us.” It was far removed from the magical scenes of the Europa League showpiece across the city.

Villa’s fears before kick-off centred on the playing surface, with the pitch recently relaid after extensive maintenance, but it had no real impact on the result. Galatasaray defeated Liverpool twice in the Champions League at Rams Park last season and can be awkward opponents.

In a game of few chances, Villa were intent on frustrating both Galatasaray’s players and supporters by slowing the game down, restricting the home team’s threat by playing five in defence.

Galatasaray were lacking inspiration but were given an injection eight minutes into the second half. The flashpoint came after a crude challenge from Davinson Sánchez on Villa’s Brazilian winger Alysson.

Sánchez, the former Tottenham defender, escaped a booking but an angry John McGinn responded by colliding with Aleksey Batrakov near the touchline. Both players were given yellow cards by Siebert, and McGinn was infuriated that Batrakov avoided more extreme punishment for kicking out at him.

That aggravation only served to fire up Galatasaray and there was a sense of inevitability to their goal 13 minutes from the end. Villa were under pressure and failed to clear a corner, with Deniz Gul punishing Jackson’s error to head the ball over the line after a deflection off Tyrone Mings.

Seven minutes of added time failed to spark Villa into life by creating a late chance and they returned home without registering a shot on Ugurcan Cakir’s goal.

Villa’s downturn in form continues with a Champions League defeat which owed everything to their shortcomings going forward. They settled well in a hostile atmosphere, but allowed all their possession to drift into sterility, and the second half was just plain poor. A low-quality game settled by a messy goal, but credit to Gul for putting his head where it hurts.

Villa will surely finish the week outside the top eight, with home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund to follow.

The referee has allowed the game on beyond the five additional minutes, but a Harwood-Bellis loose pass stalls Villa in their own half.

They soon break out into midfield space though, but with all the time in the world Barkley’s pass was a touch behind Hemmings and Sanchez was able to get a toe to it.

Of all the venues in the Champions League where a referee might be inclined to blow his whistle as soon as possible, this might be the one so time is running out for Villa.

Lucas Torreira has taken a kick on the ankle, and he limps off to be replaced by Ilkay Gundogan, who has played just 75 minutes this season.

Villa then find some space down the left but Singo blocks Maatsen’s cross which was aimed towards Jackson.

Ross Barkley the fourth Villa player booked on the night. There will be five minutes added on, which surely does not represent all of the stoppages, but Uefa’s approach to timekeeping resembles freestyle jazz.

Villa eventually worked a position to cross the ball from that free-kick, but Lindelof’s header back into the six-yard box was too close to Cakir and the goalkeeper pounced on the ball. Time running out for Villa.

Villa have been sleepwalking to defeat throughout the second half, they have completely lost any assurance in their passing game. That was better, and Goretzka wins a free-kick in midfield which they are going to clip forward.

Buendia has been brought on for Kamara, but Hemmings shoots over when Singo was on the turf appealing for a foul not given. Villa have shown more intent in the last three minutes than the previous 30.

The goalscorer Gul is back on with a bandage around part of his face.

Things could have gone from bad to worse for Aston Villa because VAR checked for a Jackson red card for a high boot on Gul, but eventually the incident is cleared. Villa have 10 minutes plus stoppage time to salvage a result.

Mbaye with a dangerous ball into the box but he was offside in any case.

Villa undone from a corner, and the striker thrown on as a substitute has scored the game’s opening goal. Gul appears to have hurt himself in the process, he took a kick in the face from Jackson when planting his head on the ball. Villa lost the first contact at the near-post and from there it was a mess. Gul receiving treatment with blood streaming down his face.

Galatasaray with a double change: Sara and Ugochukwu on for Batrakov and Lemina.

Aston Villa struggling to find any rhythm after another stoppage in the game, but Galatasaray are enjoying more of the territory. Nicolas Jackson has been a revelation this season but has been underwhelming in the second half.

Now Galatasaray have a corner! But Villa clear at the near post.

Villa floundering and under pressure for the first time in the game, Mbaye and Goretzka are about to be introduced by Emery.

Galatasaray have a free-kick in a crossing position left of centre, but Akgun’s delivery floated over everyone in the box and Torreira is then penalised for a foul on Manzambi.

Galatasaray have made a change in their attack, with a more orthodox striker in Gul replaces Elmali, so Yilmaz moves out to the left. Torreira wins a foul in midfield, but Gomes and Kamara were convinced they had won the ball cleanly.

Villa have slightly lost their way in the last 10 minutes, they are not passing the ball with their early fluency and appear caught between holding what they have or pushing on for a goal. Maatsen the latest player guilty of a cheap giveaway.

Unai Emery will be fairly satisfied with that first-half performance.

In a match of few chances, Villa have frustrated the home team and defended resolutely in the rare occasions Galatasaray have applied pressure.

Akgun wins a free-kick for Galatasaray, who have grown into the contest in the last few minutes. Torreira and Batrakov swapping positions in midfield, and Singo is an impressive player at right-back. The delivery from the free-kick is poor though.

Villa get the game under way, and from the aerial view you can see the seams between patches of the pitch.

Villa have made a solid start on their return to the Champions League, winning three and losing one.

Villa face a daunting pair of home games against Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund in their next two league phase matches.

Six months after the glory of winning the Europa League final in Istanbul, Aston Villa are back on the banks of the Bosphorus.

A potentially tricky match awaits against the Turkish champions, with much of the pre-match scrutiny on the state of the pitch.

Villa were unable to train on Rams Park on Monday as the club is undertaking repair work to the surface.

Aston Villa supporters have happy memories of Istanbul after May’s Europa League final, and they return to face Galatasaray this evening in a fixture which could forecast their Champions League prospects.

It has been par for the course for Unai Emery’s team in Europe so far, with victories over Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking and a defeat at Barcelona aligning with the form book.

Nine points from 12 leaves them inside the top eight at the halfway stage of the league phase, but tougher challenges are ahead with PSG and Borussia Dortmund to come after tonight’s game.

Since a statement victory over Manchester City, it has been a frustrating time for Villa either side of the international break. They were dumped out of the League Cup by Bournemouth, were second-best in a home draw with Fulham, threw away a pair of two-goal leads at Old Trafford, and were held by Sunderland at the weekend.

Though Villa put six past Galatasaray’s city rivals Fenerbahce at Villa Park, away games against Turkish opposition can be different beasts, as Liverpool discovered in the last round of Champions League matches.

Galatasaray’s two major attacking threats, Victor Osimhen and Rafael Leão, are both absent with injuries. Davinson Sanchez and Lucas Torreira are former Premier League players in their squad. Galatasaray have won two of four Champions League games, losing to Barcelona and Sporting Lisbon, but they are top of the Turkish Super Lig.

Villa will be without right-back Matty Cash owing to a concussion sustained during the international break with Poland, but will hope to have Victor Lindelof available again after he missed the Sunderland draw with illness.

Emery’s team were unable to train at Rams Park yesterday in order to give a troublesome pitch maximum recovery time after emergency renovation work.

“If we could have trained in the stadium of Galatasaray, maybe we would have decided for the same situation, but it’s not changing our routine,” Emery said. “How the pitch is going to be tomorrow is important, but it’s not an excuse because it’s [the same] for both teams. Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible.”

#893. Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

#892. WSL makes agreement with clubs to avoid gambling sponsors

Clubs have agreed to prioritise sponsorship deals with companies in other industries

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

WSL Football, the organisation responsible for operating the top two tiers of women’s football in the UK, has reached an agreement in principle for its clubs not to make sponsorship deals with betting companies.

Instead, the organisation has agreed to pursue sponsorship deals with brands from different industries, reports The Athletic. The outlet states that six additional sponsorship opportunities were made available ahead of the 2024/25 season, and these were filled by Apple, Airbnb, British Gas, Mercedes, Tesco and WTW.

While the agreement applies to WSL Football’s own commercial partnerships, it does not stop individual WSL or WSL2 clubs from signing sponsorship deals with gambling companies.

Rather, it sets a different direction for WSL Football’s league-level partnerships, giving the leagues the chance to shape their own commercial future. The organisation wants to continue aiding the growth of the women’s domestic game, while combating issues such as player welfare, gambling-related online abuse and fluctuating attendances.

The changes also come at a time when English football is starting to take a wider look at gambling and related sponsorships. At the start of this season, the Premier League’s voluntary ban on betting sponsors appearing on the front of match-day shirts came into effect, while the Premier League, EFL, FA and WSL also introduced a Code of Conduct for gambling-related sponsorship agreements in 2024.

Nevertheless, betting companies still feature prominently among sponsors at clubs throughout the top divisions in the men’s game, with Betway signing a deal with Manchester United and clubs such as Leeds and Nottingham Forest also agreeing new deals over the summer.

Jude Bellingham has played down comparisons to Real Madrid legend Zinedine Zidane after inspiring victory in the Champions League with a sensational goal against PSV.

The win maintains Madrid’s perfect Champions League record, elevating them to serious contenders to dethrone two-time defending champions Paris Saint-Germain, while rising up The Independent’s power rankings.

But Bellingham was quick to distance himself from the conversation, instead placing the France manager in an entirely different category.

"It popped up nicely and I thought I'm just going to hit it. So yeah, it was a nice goal and important for the team, being the second goal, and gave us control.

Mourinho was left stunned by his player’s latest impact, pinpointing just what makes him so good.

#888. Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms are needed.

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts."

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

"The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough."

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

As of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

But Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles."

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive."

The new rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Steinert said fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert said.  However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank said that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns."

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat said Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards."

This article was originally written in German.

Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid are the only teams to still have 100 per cent records after Liverpool’s defeat at Fenerbahce

It was largely business as usual last month in the Champions League as Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona kept on scoring and Arsenal and Bayern Munich returned to winning ways while remaining unbeaten.

But the story of the round belonged to Como, who made history by beating Lens 9-1 away from home and equalling the record for the most goals scored in a single Champions League game. Cesc Fabregas’s impressive side now sit fourth in the league phase standings, behind PSG, Real Madrid and Arsenal.

Meanwhile, there was a frustrating defeat for Liverpool at Fenerbahce, but Manchester United produced a stunning comeback to beat Roma and potentially save Michael Carrick’s job, with Matheus Cunha scoring twice on a remarkable night at Old Trafford.

We compiled our 36-team power rankings by combining team’s previous performance in the Champions League, their results in the competition so far, and the likelihood of them going all the way this season.

Agree or disagree with our standings ahead of matchweek five? Let us know and have your say in the comments below.

The reigning champions are making a mockery of suggestions that they are slow starters in the Champions League. Luis Enrique’s back-to-back champions finished outside the top eight in both of their previous successes but have started this campaign on fire in Europe. PSG were 4-0 up after just 17 minutes at Villarreal, and that was without Ousmane Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. The French champions will be without the brilliant Georgian for the rest of the season after he suffered a ruptured ACL and has been joined on the sidelines by Desire Doue, who suffered the same injury during a 3-2 win over Nice on Saturday.

Defeats to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League and Real Madrid in LaLiga ended their winning start under Hansi Flick and perhaps raised the same concerns over whether their defence holds up come the knockout stages. But Lamine Yamal is arguably the world’s best player on current form and Raphinha isn’t too bad, either. The Brazilian made it an astonishing 19 goals and three assists in just 13 matches across LaLiga and the Champions League with his double in the 3-0 win over Aston Villa at Camp Nou.

Mikel Arteta’s got the result they needed in Prague, even if a difficult second-half performance made it a bit of a struggle. An entertaining draw last time out at Bayern Munich, who have such a strong home record, gave a good account of whether the Premier League champions can take the next step against a heavyweight side in the business end of the Champions League. A frustrating stalemate with Dortmund brings them back into a scrap to secure that coveted top eight position, rather than a top-two seed and home advantage throughout the knockout stages.

Bayern returned to winning ways with a professional win against Atletico Madrid – and the big surprise was that Harry Kane was not on the scoresheet. The Ballon d’Or holder’s 10-match scoring run in the Champions League came to an end at the Metropolitano, missing the chance to equal Cristiano Ronaldo’s record, and Kane will now be out until the “business end” of the season due to an ankle injury.

Perhaps chaos is the new normal under Jose Mourinho. Real Madrid trailed late on in Athens but Kylian Mbappe equalised before Fede Valverde scored a stunning winner in stoppage time. Jude Bellingham also scored an outrageous flick. Somehow with maximum points, despite trailing Roma 3-1 at the Stadio Olimpico, and Inter and RB Leipzig spurning chances to take the lead at the Bernabeu, the 15-time Champions League winners continue to find a way. Romping to a 5-1 win over PSV, despite trailing, shows the firepower this team still has.

Three defeats from four in the Premier League have the shine off an impressive start for Enzo Maresca’s side, while uncertainty off the pitch remains as well. But a battling win at RB Leipzig, with a customary Erling Haaland goal, was a good response, even if City have now gone nine games without a clean sheet in all competitions. Another sloppy performance with the return of Kevin De Bruyne and Napoli, City now face a mouthwatering trip to Barcelona and likely require a result to avoid dropping out of the top eight.

Liverpool have conceded three goals in three consecutive games in the Champions League or European Cup for the first time and the manner of their “messy” collapse against Fenerbahce was a concern. The nature of Liverpool’s squad means Andoni Iraola has needed to rotate in Champions League but Liverpool’s performance in Istanbul underlined the task he faces. In-form Club Brugge can’t be taken lightly after the international break.

WOW. If Como announced themselves by thrashing Manchester United, the Champions League debutants stole the show this week with a NINE-goal dismantling of poor Lens. Cesc Fabregas’s stylish side became the first team to score nine goals away from home in the Champions League or European Cup since 1971. The Italian side are certainly making a name for themselves. Those games against PSG and Barcelona at the end of the league phase are going to be fascinating.

After starting with back-to-back defeats, how badly Inter needed to respond with back-to-back wins. A comfortable win at Feyenoord also came after the Milan derby defeat, with Pio Esposito stepping up amid Lautaro Martinez’s continued absence.

Defeat in Istanbul followed defeat at the Camp Nou puts Unai Emery’s new-look Aston Villa in a tricky spot: outside of the top eight and heading towards the playoff round. Bright showings from the refreshed attacking line-up of Nicolas Jackson, Johan Manzambi, Ibrahim Mbaye and Alysson have helped the Europa League winners retaining their identity under Emery despite the huge squad turnover in the summer, but the closing three fixtures will be tough, and they may have to settle for an additional tie in the knockout stage.

#885. Rasmus Hojlund reveals intense Bruno Fernandes reaction to Michael Carrick sacking

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Hojlund, who scored for Napoli in Manchester against City on Tuesday, is still in touch with former Man United teammate Fernandes and the pair discussed the fallout from Carrick’s dismissal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bruno Fernandes was devastated Michael Carrick was sacked as Manchester United manager, according to his former teammate Rasmus Hojlund.

The Napoli striker, who completed his £44m move away from Old Trafford in the summer, is convinced that his old team, who are 19th in the Premier League, will only have a temporary stay in the relegation zone.

And Hojlund, a boyhood United fan who joined them for £64m in 2023, believes they have too much quality to go down.

The Denmark international was back in Manchester to score for Napoli against City in Tuesday’s 2-2 draw in the Champions League.

And he said: “I am watching all the games I can, especially from the red side of Manchester. It is unfortunate [that United are struggling].”

United have not won in their last nine league games, dating back to August, and lost 4-0 to Liverpool on Sunday in Mauricio Pochettino’s first match in charge.

They are second from bottom but Hojlund is not worried. “It is a temporary picture, I think they will get back to the top, the Premier League is like this,” he said. “I read the other day that Bournemouth were in the relegation zone after a couple of games, now they have won the last five games and are in the top half of the table.

“They have got a lot of quality, I have seen the guys training day by day and I know the players really well and they have got a great squad, good leaders, good professionals so I am sure they will turn it around. Hopefully they will get it right with Mauricio.”

Captain Fernandes was dropped by Carrick after questioning his tactics in the Champions League defeat to Como but he and Diogo Dalot caught up with Hojlund when Denmark faced Portugal and the forward said they were upset the manager was losing his job.

“In the international break when I spoke with Bruno and Diogo, they were all obviously devastated that Michael was going but also looking forward to some change,” Hojlund added. “I am still speaking with Patrick [Dorgu, his Denmark teammate] and I just wish the guys all the best and I am sure they will turn it around this season.”

Hojlund, who scored 26 goals in 95 games in two seasons at Old Trafford, said playing for United comes with great pressure, making it harder in the bad times.

“United is a massive club and you can’t take anything away from that,” he said. “There are so many people following the club around the world and you can’t really escape from it, it is almost too high when it is good and almost too low when it is bad so it is all about trying to be in that middle and now I think I tried both the highs and the lows there. The pressure is part of the club. It comes with playing for Man United.”

#884. Arsenal get the best and worst of Gyokeres on frustrating night for Arteta

Mikel Arteta may prefer to imagine his Arsenal team as a remorseless winning machine, although on nights such as these they can still demonstrate a familiar unreliability when it comes to the main purpose of it all.

There were 30 shots over the night from the English champions, only four of which were on target, and in the end their winner never came. Even in the 95th minute, Arteta’s players were still conspiring to foul it up. This Champions League game might have been decided in Arsenal’s favour within 20 minutes. By half-time it should have been a formality. Yet, as chance after chance slipped away, there was always a possibility this would end differently.

The leaders of the Bundesliga were traumatised at times by the ferocity of the Arsenal press, and there were times when Borussia Dortmund will likely have no idea how they survived. Even so, they did just that and, liberated in the second half, Maximilian Beier scored an improbable equaliser in his team’s best period. There were still 40 minutes for Arsenal to put this one to bed and they found many ways not to do so.

It was notable that the man who put Arsenal ahead in the ninth minute with a right-footed thump from space on the edge of the Dortmund box was the same striker who would miss the best chance to win it. That is the Viktor Gyökeres dilemma. In the space of a single game he can look like a potential match-winner and also the last man his manager would wish to see arriving on the end of a perfect Martin Odegaard cross.

So it proved after 75 minutes when Gyökeres thrust himself at an Odegaard ball into the box that just needed guiding inside a post, yet planted it decisively wide of the mark. On the touchline Arteta tried very hard to hide his despair and failed to do so.

It ended that way, with a heroic defensive performance from the Dortmund defence, including one memorable moment when substitute Serhou Guirassy’s determination to block a cross prompted a double ricochet off his own post. One could make the argument that there were times when it was “unbelievable”, as Arteta later said, that the ball did not find its way in. Although there were also moments when the reasons were self-evident.

“There’s an element of luck,” the Arsenal manager said, “and there is an element of us [not] finishing better.”

In fifth place in the league phase table, dropped points at home do not carry the same jeopardy in the group stage that they once did, yet even so there was a truth for Arteta to chew upon. This is a well-honed, big-game Arsenal Champions League side that he has built. One that reached the final last season and may well go close again, but as ever they seem to be doing so in spite of the great goalscorer that so many of their nearest rivals have at their disposal.

Arteta sounded that warning after defeat in the final in Budapest at the end of May and, while changes have been made, it would be hard to argue that they have been fundamental. This was a good opponent – the leaders of the Bundesliga with many exports from English football who have been reconditioned for the German game. Those include Fábio Silva, Felix Nmecha and Jobe Bellingham, who had a second-half goal narrowly disallowed for offside.

Jobe Bellingham's goal RULED OUT for offside ❌ https://t.co/yaR8EX4Gs3

After a chastening first half in which they found themselves in the teeth of the Arsenal press, Dortmund re-emerged as a much more effective attacking force. They found a way to break the Arsenal press by targeting Christos Tzolis and the run from the teenage French defender Joane Gadou that followed was exceptional. That created the goal for Beier, one of four shots on target from Dortmund – the same number as Arsenal.

Maximilian Beier punishes Arsenal to make it 1-1 😳 https://t.co/OOUmg9JnHo

Dortmund, managed by the West German-born Croat Niko Kovac, did not always have Arsenal’s polish in possession but they certainly had the youth in their legs to match the English champions. In defence their captain Nico Schlotterbeck and Waldemar Anton will not have many better games. They might have been fortunate at times but they will also point to a penalty that was not given, when Gyökeres handled in his own area at the start of the second half.

Gyökeres’s first-half goal was certainly among the best he has scored for the club, invited to shoot by a Dortmund defence that simply stood off as he reached the edge of the area. He will not catch many as full as he did this one. More of a dig than a swish but with the useful consequence of packing a lot of power and a dip that meant goalkeeper Gregor Kobel saw it but could not pick out its flight.

Viktor Gyökeres what a HIT! 👏🔥 https://t.co/5m6FZoE8tQ

Asked about the later Gyökeres miss, Arteta preferred to talk about other aspects of his striker’s performance. “The way he held up the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch,” Arteta said. “There was a lot to like in that performance and that’s the Viktor that we needed.”

Even so, there was some of the Gyökeres the Arsenal manager does not need as early as the end of the first half when he launched a wild shot over from Noni Madueke’s pass. Arteta was without David Raya, who has a shoulder injury and there were no guarantees that he will be back for the Manchester City game on Sunday.

There were some good moments for young Bellingham against Myles Lewis-Skelly in the first half and then a goal disallowed after the break. That came after Beier’s equaliser when Dortmund were at their counter-attacking best. In the final stages, Arsenal pressed hard for the winner and, although there were lots of shots, it would be hard to say there were lots of chances. The one that got away was the one that fell to Gyökeres.

Arteta would later call it “a brilliant performance”. It was hard to shake the feeling from some of the caveats he added that, like everyone else, what he really thought – above all – was that his team should have won.

The performance was superb and there is no question about that from the start to the end. We played against a really good side and the domination and threat was really impressive. The general feeling inside the dressing room is that we should reward ourselves with more.

I love the courage, the fluidity and the understanding with the players with and without the ball.

That’s what we want [to finish in the top eight]. We have a big game against Manchester City at home on Sunday so we need to recover really well, we have four days to do that and sustain that momentum the way we are playing and the win will come.

I think these are the best games. I’m really looking forward to it. Two draws on the bounce now and I just desperately want to win on the weekend and I know my team-mates feel the same. We are going to do everything we have to win the three points. We’re champions, we’re at home. We have a duty to perform well at the Emirates. There are things we need to improve but all in all we are going in the right direction.

I feel like the performances from us up until the last shot was incredible at times. Definitely feels like two points dropped like the other day so, having dominated so much of the game we need to take all the points.

I prefer this type of game [more open rather than against a deep defence], there are more breaks and opportunities to attack space. We it’s a low block it’s more about pass, pass, pass and wait for the right moment. I feel like we are well-suited to both types of game.

We could have scored in the second half. We could have won the game in many different ways. We played well and created a lot of chances, we deserved to win the game but sometimes it is like that.

The most important thing is that we create those chances and get shots on goal. For sure we will score goals when games are coming up.

But they are now four points off Real Madrid, who they play next, and more than likely PSG if they beat Roma tomorrow night.

Arsenal with a remarkable combination of poor finishing and bad decision-making in the final third. They ended the night with 56 touches in the Dortmund box and 29 shots, but only four of those shots were on target.

There was time for one late scramble, but at the final whistle it is the Borussia Dortmund fans celebrating the draw.

That result is going to make it very difficult for Arsenal to finish in the top two, but they will hope to have enough for a top-eight finish. They fail to win at home for the first time this season.

Dortmund had their moments, a very strong start to the second half when they could have scored more than once.

But over the piece, the story is Arsenal’s profligacy. Twenty nine shots on goal and more than two expected goals, but not enough to show for it.

Eze with a blocked shot but Arsenal do have Dortmund pushed back in their half for the final 90 seconds. Is there one more chance!

Kobel palms behind Rice’s delivery for another Arsenal corner. Feels like now or never if Arsenal are to find the winner.

Promising attack for Dortmund, but Timber blocked Karestas’s shot.

Then Arsenal go down the other end and win a corner through Hincapie’s persistence.

Gabriel tries to win a header on the edge of Dortmund’s box but gives a foul away. Odegaard’s shot was blocked in the build up, he may have been better off crossing to the back post.

Arsenal with some good football through the lines involving Odegaard and Bruno Guimaraes, but then Konsa was the wrong man in the wrong place and committed a foul. Mikel Merino has replaced Viktor Gyokeres.

Some of the venom has gone out of the Arsenal backlash since the equaliser, but they continue to probe and push numbers forward.

And Declan Rice hits the post! Brilliant slide-rule pass from Eze to release Rice into the box, and his first-time shot with his left foot cannons of the near post.

Dortmund have a throw deep in the Arsenal half now, after Kepa found himself in a tight spot and kicked to touch. Arsenal clear but Eze fails to bring them up the pitch.

Scramble in the Dortmund goal-mouth from an Arsenal free-kick, whipped in low by Odegaard right across the face of goal, kept alive by Hincapie at the back post and the ball bounced off the post when it looked like being an own goal. Kobel stays down to receive some treatment after colliding with the post.

It feels like Arsenal have restored some dominance since the changes, and after some messy play in the penalty box they have a corner. Punched clear by Kobel, before Madueke is fouled.

Arsenal crowd growing a little frustrated with Odegaard for turning down a shot at the edge of the box, and also failing to find Gyokeres with the pass.

Then Gyokeres misses a sitter! Brilliant ball from Odegaard, Gyokeres completely unmarked to meet to inswinging cross but he heads wide from six yards. Hincapie’s run maybe put him off but that would be generous.

Eze with a sloppy giveaway in his own half but Arsenal are not punished, before Rice sets the home team away with some great play in midfield. Eze feeds Gyokeres down the left, but not red player was in the six-yard box for a cross.

Then Madueke cuts inside from the right and shoots not far wide of the near post.

Arsenal’s inability to control this second half has made for a very entertaining game. Two teams going for it. Dortmund seem to accept they can’t defend their way to a result so they might as well try to attack.

Arsenal respond by throwing a couple of punches. First Eze’s shot was deflected over, before Anton made a magnificent block to deny Madueke. The game is swinging back and forth.

Jobe Bellingham wheels away in celebration thinking he has scored for Dortmund after Ryerson’s shot was saved from Kepa but the flag goes up for offside! It took Bellingham ages to realise, and his joy was cut short.

Replays show it was very, very tight indeed. The still image suggested Hincapie was playing him on, but VAR confirms offside as the decision.

To give Kepa credit, it was a sharp save.

Jobe Bellingham's goal RULED OUT for offside ❌ https://t.co/yaR8EX4Gs3

Gyokeres with more gallant work in the channels for Arsenal but he is lacking some support at times, perhaps Eze and Guimaraes can change that.

Here come a raft of changes. Guirassy and Karestas on for Dortmund, replacing Beier and Fabio Silva.

Triple sub from Arsenal: Eze, Guimaraes and Timber replace Tzolis, Lewis-Skelly and White.

Dortmund are preparing a double substitution but Arsenal have a corner. Whipped into the near post by Rice, and Konsa and Gabriel rather got in each other’s way.

The game is really good contest now, high level Champions League fare. Arsenal might need the win if they want a top-two finish.

Anton looks short of pace at the back for Dortmund, and Gyokeres streaks away from him down the left. Hincapie is the player found with the cut-back, and he tees up White for a shot that is always rising.

A flowing move but it ended at the feet of two defenders.

Arsenal in search of an instant response, withe Odegaard finding Gyokeres with a pass into feet inside the box. His shot was blocked, and then Kobel saved Hincapie’s follow up header.

Madueke is then away from the right, shrugging off Anton, but no red shirt arrives in the six-yard box to reach his cross.

Arteta has been agitated since the half-time break and he will not have been impressed by the defensive work of Tzolis there. The Greek winger allowed Gadou to burst away and then dived in ineffectively as he ran downfield. These are the details and duels that Arteta obsesses over.

Goudou with a burst away from Tzolis and straight through the middle of the Arsenal midfield, and Beier’s first touch inside Gabriel was fantastic before he finished with a left-footed shot into the bottom corner. A very well-worked equaliser.

That’s how to break the Arsenal press. Run hard at Tzolis and give it everything. Great finish from Beier but an even better run from Joane Gadou to make it.

Maximilian Beier punishes Arsenal to make it 1-1 😳 https://t.co/OOUmg9JnHo

Kepa saves a routine shot from distance but almost puts Arsenal in trouble with his throw out, and there was an almighty 50:50 between Lewis-Skelly and Nmecha. At the other end, Odegaard neglected to shoot on his right foot after he was teed up by Madueke.

Looking back at the penalty shout, Gyokeres’ arm was slightly away from his body.

Dortmund have a corner earned from a long throw, they are certainly growing into the contest now.

Cleared by Ben White at the near post, but there were loud Dortmund appeals for a handball penalty.

You never know with Uefa handball roulette, but VAR is of course checking.

Dortmund’s best move and opportunity of the game, Svensson with a low cross that beats Konsa and Beier was in front of Gabriel but he completely missed an attempted flick at the near post.

Then Madueke dances through a couple of challenges and bends a shot wide of the far post.

Kobel rushes outside of his box to clear a Gabriel pass aimed towards Tzolis. Gadou with a really poor pass across midfield when Dortmund were trying to keep position, wildly overhit which invited Arsenal to press and an aimless long ball followed.

Arsenal kick off the second 45 minutes. No changes from Arteta or Kovac.

A 70mph strike from Viktor Gyökeres against Dortmund 💨😮‍💨 https://t.co/hQHcCWvjUz

Noni Madueke has started nine of Arsenal's last 11 matches in all competitions. This run of games has had such a positive effect on him. He looks more confident, relaxed and expressive than at any point in his #AFC career. Perhaps not having the pressure of Saka has helped him.

Dortmund’s gameplan clearly based on the build-up from goalkeeper to the two centre-halves and then forward. It is a different prospect doing it in the Bundesliga to doing it against the Arsenal pressing machine and over the course of the first half Dortmund have lost their nerve in that regards. Goalkeeper Gregor Kobel has gone long to the left flank more than he would have liked. But – and it’s a significant point – they have looked quite good once they have got into Arsenal’s half. The Gyokeres goal was a good dig that beat Kobel with the dip. It was close to him. For all that Gyokeres was invited to shoot. Not a yellow shirt near by.

Arsenal much the better team across the 45 minutes, racking up 14 shots and enjoying 61 per cent possession. A familiar tale though, is their failure to convert that dominance into a commanding lead. Borussia Dortmund gradually carried more threat as the half progressed, and Arsenal cannot count on the insurance policy of Raya in goal. They need the second goal.

A moment of sloppiness from Arsenal near the end of the half, and Kepa was almost caught out at his near post but managed to make the save at the expense of a corner. Nmecha won first contact, but his header looped over.

Madueke wins the ball back high for Arsenal and finds Odegaard, but the flag goes up for offside against Arsenal’s captain. Replays suggest it was close, but Gyokeres was pleased to see the flag after missing a good chance in the middle.

Kepa patient on the ball for Arsenal to find Gabriel, who picks out Madueke with a diagonal over the top. Good close control from the winger, and he tees up Gyokeres for another attempt from just outside the box but he skies this one.

Dortmund win a corner from another Ryerson cross, he has looked their best outlet down the right. From the corner, Kepa was scrambling among bodies but Arsenal get away with it. Arteta wanted a foul on the goalkeeper.

Dortmund are a far more open opponent than Arsenal are used to facing in the Premier League, and they are fortunate not to have conceded more goals here, but they are willing to attack quite quickly in numbers. They’ve had five shots so far, and a couple of those were decent chances.

From the second phase of the next corner, Tzolis volleyed miles over when a shot was not on. Lewis-Skelly has been quietly effective in midfield for Arsenal, and there is applause for Ethan Nwaneri as he goes out to warm up for Dortmund. William Saliba is also out there stretching.

Incisive from Odegaard after Dortmund lost the ball in a dangerous position, and Rice charged straight through the middle, but was running out of steam as he took the shot and it deflected wide.

Corner taken short, well-worked between Lewis-Skelly and Tzolis, and the caught back falls for Gyokeres whose shot deflects wide for another corner.

No doubt Arsenal’s electric start of the opening 15 minutes has slowed, I’m not sure it would be possible or desirable to maintain that intensity across the 90 minutes. They are controlling the pace of and remaining patient, before Rice lets fly from almost 30 yards. Not far over the bar.

Dortmund with a nifty up, set and through but they had run offside. Gabriel then looks over the top for Hincapie, who was running over the top like a striker from left-back yet again.

Declan Rice with a crunching tackle in his own half that has the Emirates crowd on its feet, and Arsenal are flowing forward into space again but Gyokeres failed to pick the right final ball.

Now Dortmund have a corner after a Svensson shot deflects wide. Kepa claims with ease.

Hincapie, as we have seen with Arsenal’s full-backs all season, is popping up in advanced positions and he had a clear sight of goal but elected to pull the ball back when he should have put his laces through it. Well worked attack before then though, with Rice finding Odegaard between the lines and Gyokeres flicking the ball around the corner.

Better again from Dortmund, moving the ball with fluency from their own defensive third but Nmecha miscues his shot over the bar from the edge of the box. Kepa is then off his line to collect a chipped ball over the top.

Tzolis did well to harry and win the race to a long ball forward and he was close to flicking the ball into the path of Gyokeres.

Dortmund are starting to string some passes together, and they have a corner. This is one department where Arsenal will be appreciably worse without Raya but Hincapie heads clear.

Madueke then spins into space on the break and Gyokeres is free in the middle, but the winger slices the chipped pass.

Dortmund with their first attempt of the night after Ryerson swung in a cross from the left. Lewis-Skelly did well to compete in the air with Bellingham, before Silva kicked fresh air. Then with his second attempt, he volleyed over the bar.

Dortmund trying to settle into a spell of possession, but every pass feels like a chore for them at the moment and they are caught offside. Arsenal’s task now is to score the second while they have Dortmund where they want them. The German side will surely have a spell.

Gyokeres with another stretching run beyond Schlotterbeck, who is not the quickest. Arsenal completely dominant at the moment, but they do not always capitalise on these spells.

Chance for a second! Tzolis’ shot was parried by Kobel and Madueke’s rebound was blocked after he took a beat to control the ball. Could Madueke taken a swing first time?

Arsenal are well worth that opening goal. Looking back at the replays of Gyokeres’s strike, it was an unusual technique, brushing the turf before the ball much as a golfer might do with a bunker shot.

Gyokeres may lack craft at times but there is no doubt he has power. That was a superb strike, dipping towards goal with real ferocity. Arsenal don’t score many goals from range but they have plenty of players who can do it. Gyokeres now has five goals and three assists in his last 10 games for club and country.

Madueke in acres of space down the right again, and there was too much space in front of the Dortmund back three for Gyokeres to receive the ball and turn. From there, Gyokeres decided to take the shot on and his laces technique produced power and dip which deceived the goalkeeper Kobel. It was not in the corner, but the loop did for him. Similar to one or two goals Morgan Rogers scored last season.

Viktor Gyökeres what a HIT! 👏🔥 https://t.co/5m6FZoE8tQ

Dortmund find themselves beyond the halfway line for the first time in the game and there was an error from Rice that Fabio Silva failed to take advantage of. Arsenal soon back on the front foot though, and Odegaard’s shot from distance is blocked.

Noni Madueke has been Arsenal’s best attacker in recent weeks and he has started well here. He is really thriving in the absence of the injured Bukayo Saka. Perhaps that knowledge that he will start games has given him a sense of freedom that he was lacking before.

Arsenal have endured some slow starts to matches this season, but this has not been one of them. Dortmund cannot find room to breathe at the moment, and Arsenal are moving the ball with speed and authority. They are up the pitch again after Gyokeres wins a foul. Moments earlier, Madueke found Tzolis at the back post with a curling cross but Dortmund cleared his nod across goal.

Gyokeres with a scuffed shot from long range straight at the goalkeeper, but Arsenal continue to be on the front foot. Hincapie, their left-back challenged for the ball in the centre-forward position.

Very positive start from Arsenal, enjoying all of the ball in the first few minutes. Tzolis with a promising cross which was not far away from Hincapie, then Lewis-Skelly was in well to keep Dortmund pinned back. Madueke was found in space, and Tzolis connected with his ball to the back post, the volley bouncing over the ball.

Dortmund get the game under way, and line up almost all of their team on the left side of the pitch.

The entrance of players follows a pre-match light show and an airing of everyone’s favourite song The Angel, shunted back in the schedule to make room for the Champions League anthem.

You can see Jobe is developing very well. As you also saw, he is now part of the England national team now.

This is not by random, this is because he deserves it and he plays very well in the Bundesliga. Since he arrived, he’s developed day after day.

In the beginning he needed a bit of time because the differences between the Championship and Bundesliga are huge, also the cultural aspect is different. He came to a new country, he had to learn now to live in Germany, but he’s there.

I’m very happy with him. He’s progressing and not only developing physically but with the ball and this is what we need.

I’m very impressed with them, with what Niko has done with the team, especially the way they are playing, the way they are dominating games, the amount of threat that they are able to create.

We had them here in pre-season (a 3-2 defeat) and they showed their quality and what they are capable of, so we are very much aware of that.

But we play at home in front of our crowd and we’re going to go and attack the game, that’s for sure.

Mikel Arteta seems quite set on his left-back pecking order: Riccardo Calafiori starts on weekends, and Piero Hincapie starts in midweek. They are very different players (Calafiori is the more adventurous, while Hincapie is more of an old-school defender) and it seems that Arteta feels Hincapie is better suited to Champions League football. He’ll be tested tonight against the Bundesliga leaders.

By Yannick HuberOn Tuesday, all eyes will be on Ethan Nwaneri. The Champions League clash between Arsenal and Borussia Dortmund marks the 19-year-old’s return to the club where he grew up, where he became the Premier League’s youngest player and from whom he joined Dortmund on loan in the summer. It would be hard to imagine a more poignant setting. But for Nwaneri, facing Arsenal is about more than a reunion. It is also an opportunity to finally make his mark at Dortmund.

So far his time in Germany has not gone according to plan. Nwaneri arrived with a considerable reputation and high expectations, but has become less prominent in recent weeks. His playing time has diminished and he has frequently had to settle for a place on the bench.

But there are several reasons to believe that, of all games, this meeting with his former club could give his Dortmund career fresh impetus.

Arsenal: Kepa; White, Konsa, Gabriel, Hincapie; Rice, Lewis-Skelly; Madueke, Odegaard, Tzolis; GyokeresSubs: Meslier, Porter, Saliba, Mosquera, Eze, Timber, Merino, Havertz, Calafiori, Guimaraes, Dowman

Dortmund: Kobel, Ryerson, Anton, Schlotterbeck, Gadou, Svensson, Veerman, Nmecha, Bellingham, Beier, SilvaSubs: Drewes, Meyer, Bensebaini, Guirassy, Chukwuemeka, Nwaneri, Karetsas, Sabitzer, Mane, Albert, Dos Santos, Reggiani

Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player the last time they played Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League, and tonight he will have to make do without first-choice goalkeeper David Raya.

Arsenal’s manager struck an upbeat note when describing the shoulder or upper arm injury Raya sustained at Newcastle, and it appears he has avoided a long-term absence.

Even two weeks out, however, would mean Raya missing Premier League fixtures against Manchester City, Brentford and Spurs – possibly Arsenal’s most testing week of the season. Arteta did not rule out a return to face City on Sunday.

Kepa Arrizabalaga is expected to deputise against Dortmund, who are top of the Bundesliga and have won three of their four Champions League league phase games. They won at the Emirates in a pre-season friendly, and Jobe Bellingham and on-loan Arsenal attacker Ethan Nwaneri are among their ranks.

These Champions League fixtures can feel secondary in importance to Premier League fare because of the competition’s new format, but a top-two finish in the league phase is a serious incentive.

As Arsenal discovered to their benefit last season when they “won” the league phase, the top two teams are rewarded with home second legs all the way to the final.

Arsenal are currently third on 10 points and face Real Madrid at the Emirates next, the team above them in second, so victory this evening is essential to set up that occasion.

Arteta has tended to make between four and six changes for these games, and Ben White, Piero Hincapie, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Christos Tzolis and Viktor Gyokeres are players pushing for starts after starting on the bench at Newcastle.

Also among the substitutes at St James’ Park was William Saliba, who is stepping up his return from a long-term back injury and could play his first minutes of the season tonight.
