#883. Bruno Fernandes has huge question to ponder on emotional return to Sporting

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Man United captain has been one of the most visible faces of the club’s decline, yet consistently their best player – now he must decide what comes next

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

In the modern Manchester United, it sometimes seems that the bad news comes ever sooner after the good. There is less time to enjoy it before the unwanted reality check. So it was that, when much of Sky Sports descended on Carrington on Friday and chief executive Omar Berrada revealed they were in talks with Bruno Fernandes about a new deal, the question was put to the captain.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he said. And if it was a partial answer, saying that the club were keen to extend their relationship but not revealing if he was, nor was there much encouragement to be derived from his explanation. “I just put that to a side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.”

A couple of days later came a result to underline the wisdom of waiting. Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing at Liverpool increased the chances United will be in the Championship, rather than the Champions League, next season. At the least, Fernandes should put his future on hold before working out which division they will be in.

His next transfer may come next summer, when his contract expires – though United have the option to extend it by a further year – but his last move remains his January 2020 switch from Sporting CP. Wednesday night gives him a first chance return to his former club. It could be a triumphant comeback: Fernandes remains among Sporting’s greatest exports and he is still the only unqualified success in United’s recruitment since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

It was at Sporting that he started scoring at a rate that is almost unrivalled among midfielders: 33 goals in the 2018-19 season, a further 15 in a few months before United made their move.

Almost seven years on, Fernandes goes back on the brink of milestones: one away from a century of Portugal caps, a hat-trick short of 200 club career goals, the last 113 of them for United.

But individual achievements seem to outnumber the collective feats. That is no criticism: at times it has felt as though Fernandes has prevented things from getting worse for United. He has won the FA Cup and the Carabao Cup but, in other eras, that would not be much to show for seven seasons at Old Trafford.

He won the PFA Player of the Year and Footballer of the Year awards last season; they had the air of lifetime achievement awards, as much as recognition for his record-breaking tally of 21 Premier League assists. He has won United’s player-of-the-year award a record five times: but previously, there was more competition. Paul Scholes, for example, never won it.

The contrarian notion United would be better off without him looks increasingly fanciful when the shortcomings of others are ever more apparent. Fernandes has a petulant streak and a capacity to give the ball away in his attempts to make something happen; yet when he criticised Michael Carrick’s tactics after the defeat to Como and the manager responding by benching his skipper, United were hopeless against Bournemouth.

Mauricio Pochettino marked his arrival at Old Trafford by confirming Fernandes as hius captain. He has now worn the armband under eight managers or caretakers – Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Ralf Rangnick, Erik ten Hag, Ruud van Nistelrooy, Ruben Amorim, Darren Fletcher, Carrick and Pochettino – whereas arguably United’s greatest captain, Roy Keane, only did so under one.

It is another indication of instability and underachievement. As Fernandes implied on Friday, he has made sacrifices to stay at United. He could have had a warmer climate elsewhere, he said. He could have made more money, too: the Saudi Pro-League, in particular, would have been more lucrative. Galatasaray might have been.

The sense, perhaps, is that Fernandes, more than United, has to decide what comes next. In footballing lexicon, players earn new contracts. Maybe, though, the club have to earn the right for a deal that is proffered to be signed.

Fernandes will turn 33 next September. His next contract will probably be the last at anything near his peak, even for a man who, since the start of the 2017-18 season, has averaged over 60 games a year for club and country.

And yet, he may note, he might have played more in the Champions League simply by staying at Sporting. They were quarter-finalists last season, when United were not in the competition. They are three points ahead of United now. They stand a far better chance of being in the Champions League next season.

Fernandes has been one of the most visible faces in the decline of United, but also the man who did more than anyone else to fight it. It has given him a form of greatness but perhaps, as he returns to Portugal, it could make him ponder the career choices he has made, and will make.

#882. Helsinki puts trust at the heart of its smart-city model

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Benjamin Plackett is a science journalist based in London.

Helsinki Central Library Oodi is just one example of a building in the Finnish capital that uses real-time data to optimize energy efficiency.Credit: Sergei Gapon/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

Urban planners — and curious residents — can go online and click on almost any building in Helsinki to see a host of details including its age, height, heating source and estimated energy use. The information sits in the various maps that make up Helsinki 3D, an open-data digital twin of the city built by the City of Helsinki from aerial photographs, light and detection laser scanning (LiDAR) surveys, housing registers and geographical data. The project’s Energy and Climate Atlas estimates heating demand for nearly every building, models how it would change in response to different climate conditions and calculates the solar-panel potential across every roof and wall in the Finnish capital.

Helsinki’s technical prowess in these kinds of projects is underpinned by a substantial research base; the city is ranked 100th among the world’s top 200 cities in the Nature Index, with particular strength in health sciences (ranked 69th), biological sciences (80th) and Earth and environmental sciences (83rd). It produced 55% of Finland’s total Share in 2025, a ratio that is among the highest for cities in the overall top 200.

The city has treated itself as a laboratory, too. Kalasatama, a brownfield site in the harbour district of Helsinki, has been designated as an urban testbed for researchers, city officials and companies to try out novel urban infrastructure ideas.

Helsinki’s Nordic climate is also an advantage when it comes to handling the large amounts of data involved with smart cities. Cooler air reduces the energy needed to chill large data centres and the excess warmth created by such facilities is redirected to residents using heat pumps. One of the largest data-centre operators that publishes its waste heat recovery data says it recovers up to 90% of its waste heat, which is fed into the district heating network — enough to warm 14,000 two-room apartments.

One of Helsinki’s most distinct smart-city features is the way it uses data.

“We have to be responsible when we use AI. We must do it in a transparent way,” says Pasi Rautio, a service manager for the City of Helsinki’s AI and optimization unit.

The city’s AI register, for example, allows residents to keep tabs on AI projects the city’s government is running. It shows what data are being used and why, and offers the opportunity for public feedback.

Manchester United are in the market for a central defender and Mauricio Pochettino understands the need better than most

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

The long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.

#880. Bayern Munich insist Jamal Musiala’s health is ‘top priority’ following criticism

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The German champions have moved to address speculation surrounding the midfielder’s recovery after criticism from FIFPRO

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bayern Munich have insisted that Jamal Musiala’s health remains their "top priority" following a "constructive meeting" with representatives of the 23-year-old midfielder.

Earlier this year, the player collapsed on two occasions within four days during pre-season fixtures. It was subsequently disclosed that he was suffering from absence seizures linked to a form of "neurological dysfunction".

The German club faced scrutiny over their handling of the matter after public remarks from senior figures. Honorary president Uli Hoeness questioned if Musiala would "regain the performance level he once had", suggesting his 2025 contract might no longer match his potential on-pitch contributions.

Similar doubts were voiced by member of the supervisor board Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who proposed renegotiating the agreement, while chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen questioned the deal, should Musiala struggle to recover his peak conditioning.

These comments drew criticism from global players’ union FIFPRO, which voiced concern over repeated public remarks challenging the player's contract, saying that "a club of Bayern’s standing should know better".

Responding on Wednesday after Tuesday's discussions, Bayern sought to clarify their position in a joint update with Musiala's agency, 11WINS.

The club stated: "Yesterday, Tuesday, FC Bayern Munich held a constructive meeting with Jamal Musiala’s management. The player’s health is the top priority for both parties. Jamal Musiala will receive full support throughout his recovery.

"Following numerous rumours over the past few days, FC Bayern and 11WINS, the agency representing Jamal Musiala, would like to clarify the following: Jamal Musiala was first examined for symptoms resembling absence seizures on 22 April 2025. This examination took place in consultation with FC Bayern and its medical department, immediately after the neurological symptoms first appeared.

"FC Bayern and Jamal Musiala’s management have agreed to continue their discussions in a spirit of partnership and confidentiality."

On the pitch, Musiala returned as a substitute during last Friday's 1-1 draw against Cologne, marking his first outing since September after recovering from a hamstring injury. He has also been selected in Bayern's squad to play Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.

Arsenal wonderkid Ethan Nwaneri hasn't established himself on loan - and now faces further competition for his place

Ethan Nwaneri's Arsenal career appears to be floundering, with the on-loan Borussia Dortmund teenager facing a further transfer setback.

Nwaneri returns to his parent club tonight in the Champions League with the Bundesliga giants and is eligible to face Arsenal despite still being owned by the Gunners.

But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.

Nwaneri became the Premier League's youngest-ever player in 2022 at the age of 15 – with Max Dowman later taking that record – before establishing himself in the 2024/25 season as a serious option on the right wing for the Gunners.

But after going out on loan at Marseille last term and heading to Dortmund this time, the teenager is yet to impress, with Arteta even admitting this week that “moments are not enough” for Nwaneri in his development and that consistency must follow.

A report from Sport Witness, likewise, reads as bad news for the 19-year-old, with the Gunners now pursuing a move for Gilberto Mora as soon as January.

Mora was the youngest player selected for the 2026 World Cup and has impressed hugely in his native Mexico, courting the attention of virtually every big club in Europe.

In attacking midfield areas, Arsenal already have the likes of Martin Odegaard, Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Max Dowman – with the latter two options on the wing – and should Arsenal bring in another teenage talent, Nwaneri's first-team opportunities would appear even scarcer.

FourFourTwo understands that the Gunners were open to offers for the starlet over the summer, opting to retain him and develop him at one of the best finishing schools in European football, though the paths of Nwaneri and Hale End colleague Myles Lewis-Skelly have been drastically different, thanks, in part, due to competition for places.

With Liverpool also circling for Mora, however, the Gunners may well have to present a particularly enticing package to secure the 18-year-old.

According to the report, the youngster has a release clause of around €25 million, making any move for him particularly costly – and suggesting that the Gunners could well incorporate him into their first team immediately.

Nwaneri, meanwhile, is valued by Transfermarkt at €25m. Arsenal return to Champions League action tonight against Dortmund at the Emirates Stadium.

#877. Jose Mourinho reveals unusual half-time team talk that sparked Real Madrid’s Champions League comeback

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Real Madrid trailed at the break on Tuesday before scoring five unanswered goals after half time

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Following Real Madrid's turnaround victory against PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League, Jose Mourinho revealed his unusual half-time team talk that sparked his team’s second-half onslaught.

Asked how he inspired his side after trailing 1-0 at the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium on Tuesday, Mourinho initially wanted to keep his methods under wraps as he joked: "The locker room is like (Las) Vegas, what happens in Vegas stays in Vegas,"

Jude Bellingham, introduced as a substitute to spark the Madrid attack, later admitted the manager was understandably "a bit angry" following a disappointing opening period.

Rather than relying solely on a dressing-room row, Mourinho selected images to highlight his side’s positional mistakes. The tactical correction paid immediate dividends, with Madrid scoring five unanswered goals after the break to secure a 5-1 win, maintaining a perfect record with five consecutive European victories this term.

"I saw a terrible first half and tried with the analysts to find three or four images that could show the players exactly what we were doing wrong," Mourinho explained. "It was a half time with few words because a picture is worth a thousand words. We looked at three different images, one from a defensive perspective and two from an offensive perspective. I think with visualisation, it’s much easier for the players to understand."

The manager noted that the visual breakdown prompted an immediate "mental click" across the squad. Goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois agreed, adding: "On the screen you could see clearly that we weren’t doing things right and they were,"

Mourinho reshuffled his line-up drastically at the interval, making three changes including a double swap in central defence and introducing Bellingham, who had been rested from the start. The England midfielder’s arrival "proved key" to the outcome as he scored once and assisted another, with his manager noting he "gave the team a completely different dynamic."

Federico Valverde levelled the score five minutes after the restart, before Bellingham produced a striking effort 10 minutes later to put Madrid ahead. Kylian Mbappé then struck twice before Vinícius Júnior wrapped up the scoring late on, assisted by Bellingham.

Before the interval, PSV had exploited Madrid's defensive gaps through swift counter-attacks, alarming the home fans - including newly appointed board member Rafael Nadal and his son - as the Dutch visitors created repeated openings.

To fix the defensive frailties, Mourinho withdrew Éder Militão and Antonio Rüdiger for Dean Huijsen and Ibrahima Konaté, while Bellingham replaced Aurélien Tchouaméni. He also adjusted the tactical roles of Arda Güler and Bernardo Silva.

"The players at the back also felt much more comfortable pressing high," Mourinho said. "PSV gave us a hard time in the first half, and we struggled to win the ball back. In the second half, we had absolute control, and when the players up front wake up and start playing with joy, what happened can happen."

Mbappé’s double made him the second-youngest player to reach 75 Champions League goals after Lionel Messi, reaching the mark in 103 games - the third-fastest behind Messi and Robert Lewandowski, according to Uefa statistics.

Meanwhile, Vinícius scored his 87th-minute strike to record just his second goal of the campaign for Madrid, and his first since August.

#876. Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, says women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

Enzo Maresca had two home games in four days to get Manchester City into decent shape for Sunday’s clash against Arsenal, which now feels like a must-win. On Tuesday, however, they ended up being taunted by Rasmus Hojlund on another evening that raised more questions than answers.

Max Allegri, a manager under pressure, will be reasonably satisfied with the first half an hour away from home for his side. He will though want to see more from his side going forward.

They do create an opening on the right side of the penalty area but Politano’s ball across cannot find a teammate. Politano was put into that good position courtesy of a great first-time pass from De Bruyne.

Two former Manchester United men combine down Napoli’s left as McTominay feeds it forward into the path of Hojlund, whose shot from the left side of the box is straight at Donnarumma.

Napoli have not really threatened the Man City goal and the hosts seem to have a reasonable control on this game but the home fans are very, very quiet and subdued. The only noise really is coming from the away fans. Man City have been a bit slow in possession and have lacked some urgency in their play.

Cherki’s step-over takes him past Lang with ease and is then brought down by the latter just outside the Napoli box on the right. Fernandez fires it low but it is a poor delivery as Gilmour easily clears at the front post.

Haaland goes down inside the Napoli penalty area, wanting a penalty, before Allan has a shot blocked. Olivera had his arms around Haaland as the cross came in from the right but VAR does not intervene. Olivera was taking a risk with that but was the contact enough to take Haaland down to the ground, that is the question?

The travelling Napoli fans are certainly making their voices heard inside the Etihad. They are currently making far more noise than the home supporters.

Enzo Maresca did confirm before the game that Cherki would start wide right and so that has proven. Brazilian forward Allan is out on the left with Fernandez playing in the ten role behind Haaland.

Should O’Reilly have done better with that chance? Nunes clips in a first-time cross from the right which picks out O’Reilly, whose header from eight yards out misses the target.

That was a nervy moment for Man City. Napoli captain Politano clips in a dangerous free-kick from the left to the back post, where McTominay tries to get on the end of it. However, Anderson gets a touch on it before the last touch comes off McTominay. Initially, a corner was given but that is overturned with McTominay touching it last.

Moments later, McTominay has a shot blocked from the left side of the box which goes behind for a corner. De Bruyne, who receives some applause as he goes over to take it, sends the corner too far and the ball goes behind for a goal kick.

The first corner of the night goes the way of the hosts as Anderson’s cross from the right is blocked by Olivera and spins behind for a corner. Interestingly, Napoli have left three players up the pitch.

Man City take it short, with Anderson and Fernandez working it well before the latter has a shot blocked inside the Napoli penalty area.

You would not call Napoli a side in form. Max Allegri’s men have just six wins from 16 games in the league and Champions League so far this season. Manchester City have failed to win any of their last four league games but have won three from four in this competition.

The first chance of the night goes the way of the hosts. Anderson shoots from range and forces Napoli keeper Milinkovic-Savic into a fairly routine save down to his right. Anderson scored a good goal at the weekend in Man City’s draw against Fulham but that effort did not have enough power on it to trouble the Napoli keeper.

Khaldoon Al-Mubarak is here, sat next to Uefa president Aleksander Čeferin.....

After Kevin De Bruyne exchanges plenty of hugs with some former teammates, both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off at the Etihad. A banner for De Bruyne is unveiled. There are a lot of empty seats at the Etihad this evening. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Manchester City: Donnarumma; Nunes, Guéhi, Gvardiol, O’Reilly; Bouaddi, Anderson; Cherki, Fernandez, Allan; Haaland.Substitutes: Rulli, Ndiaye, Kovačić, Doku, Aït-Nouri, Reis, Khusanov, Foden, McAidoo, Samba, Lewis.

City will be wearing an orange kit tonight, a special edition in collaboration with fashion brand CP Company. Napoli are also wearing away colours so it will not look much like City v Napoli when they players head out of the tunnel.

How much are Man City missing Kevin De Bruyne? 🤔 Joleon Lescott gives his verdict 👀 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/pogjeOi00P

It is not just Kevin De Bruyne in this Napoli side who is used to the Premier League. In total, there are four former Premier League players in their starting XI; De Bruyne, Rasmus Hojlund, Billy Gilmour and Scott McTominay. On the bench is then former Fulham midfielder André-Frank Zambo Anguissa.

Napoli appear depleted. They have only named seven subs and two of those are goalkeepers. But their midfield has a familiar Premier League look to it with Kevin De Bruyne starting alongside Billy Gilmour and Scott McTominay.

Aston Villa have made the trip out to Istanbul to face Galatasaray and are currently 1-0 down. You can follow the closing stages to that match right here.

Meanwhile in north London, Arsenal host Borussia Dortmund, with that game kicking off at 8pm.

“I am proud of what I have done as a football player, and honestly, this is my club, I love the owners. I have even spoken to [chairman] Khaldoon [Al Mubarak] about how to buy a club. I have nothing but affection for this club, and that will never change, [the way] the people treated me and my family for 10 years.

“Of course, in life there are rules, but everybody plays on the limit. I played in between the white lines, and I competed with other players, and I had many experiences with my teams, with the players. That is the thing that I value most. I have given my all and that is not going to change in my mind. I do not think a lot of people will change in their mind how they view me as a player, or how we played. But everybody has their own opinion, I guess. Other people may be ‘disgraced’ a bit, but I cannot change anything about that.”

Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

De Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

At Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury issues, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

“Not a lot I can say for the moment,” said De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

“There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”

It is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

Manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

“We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca said. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is important to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”

Napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

“This match will not be decisive,” Allegri said. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily. We will have to be able to play both with and without possession.”

Team news from the Etihad to follow shortly.

#873. Newcastle’s Saudi owners PIF pursue selling significant part of club

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Independent's journalism is supported by our readers. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn commission.

Saudi Arabia’s PIF are open to selling a quarter of the club through new shares five years after a consortium completed a takeover of the Premier League giants

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Public Investment Fund (PIF), Newcastle United’s majority owner, is exploring a potential sale of 25 per cent of the Premier League club through new shares.

Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and a consortium completed a takeover in October 2021, but JP Morgan has now been appointed as advisors to handle the partial sale.

As first reported by The Athletic, the minority stake is now available to buyers to secure better investment in Newcastle’s infrastructure projects, including a potential new stadium or the expansion of St James' Park.

No funds would be directed to the PIF, though the Saudis’ existing stake would be diluted through the share issue.

The PIF jointly-bought Newcastle from Mike Ashley for £305m in 2021, with the PIF’s Yasir Al-Rumayyan serving as Newcastle’s chairman.

Al-Rumayyan attended his first match of the season on Saturday in the 2-2 draw with Arsenal.

The potential deal could allow the Saudis to secure fresh investment in the club without deviating from a long-term commitment.

The PIF’s investment in sport has evolved in 2026, having ended its investment and the financing of the LIV Golf series, which collapsed and ultimately went into bankruptcy.

In addition to a new stadium, Newcastle’s long-term ambition includes a new training complex near the city’s international airport.

Are the Premier League’s London clubs at an advantage? Arsenal prepare to put that unique theory to the test

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Having made their longest Premier League away trip of the season to Newcastle last week, Arsenal can settle into familiar surroundings for the festive period: the Gunners don’t leave London again until mid-January when they travel to Hull.

Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

That’s the third of 11 straight games in the capital for the Gunners, which will become 12 if they’re drawn at home in the third round of the FA Cup, beginning with Tuesday’s Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund. Recent history suggests an interesting theory about such home comforts.

Eleven games into their title defence, Arsenal sit second in the Premier League away table with four wins, one draw and one defeat from six games on the road. Not that it’s anything new for the Gunners to occupy such heights: they’ve boasted the top flight’s best away record in each of the last four seasons.

And that comes with the territory of being a London club. Across the last 10 Premier League campaigns not impacted by pandemic crowd restrictions (so excluding 2019/20 and 2020/21), only once have more clubs from London had a bottom-half away record than a top-half away record. That was last term, when four of the seven London clubs finished in the bottom 10 of the away table (Crystal Palace, Brentford, Fulham and West Ham).

In each of the other nine seasons in question, at least 57 per cent of the Premier League’s London clubs have finished with one of the best 10 away records in the division; in 2016/17, all five of them did (Chelsea, Tottenham, Arsenal, Palace and West Ham).

So, is it an advantage to be a London club?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There’s not really a simple answer to that question (sorry), but we can still pull together some interesting takeaways.

This season, the average Premier League club will travel 153 kilometres for an away fixture. For two clubs, that average climbs to over 300km: the league’s two most north-easterly sides, Sunderland (350km) and Newcastle (347km), and the most south-westerly, Bournemouth (317km). Conversely, one side will travel a touch under 200km on average: Coventry (198km) – in that sense, you might consider the Sky Blues the ultimate Midlands club.

But the top-flight’s six London clubs all sit in the bottom eight of the league in terms of average away travel distance, with Palace travelling the furthest (227km) and Spurs the least far (202km). And the very fact that those sides account for just over a quarter of the division means short trips are a regular occurrence.

And for Arsenal, this 11-match stretch that sees them go no further than Brentford could not fall at a better time than the notoriously hectic festive period – certainly when it comes to maximising recovery time between fixtures, which come thick and fast an average of one game every 4.2 days between now and January 5 (though it’s worth noting that turnaround is still below the UEFA-recommended minimum window of five days between matches).

Could the timing of Arsenal’s London residency, so to speak, prove crucial to another successful Premier League title push? Well, they’re already six points clear at the top and look like they could walk it, given Manchester City’s dramatic recent drop-off, but minimising time spent on the road during one of the busiest stages of the campaign seems unlikely to work to their detriment.

That being said, a quick word on Chelsea: the Blues have left London three times all season but are languishing in mid-table in the Premier League and are out of the Carabao Cup. So, maybe there’s something to be said for getting out of town on a more regular basis. Besides, it’s not like elite-level players these days are travelling in anything less than luxury, is it?

Tom Hancock started freelancing for FourFourTwo in April 2019 and has also written for the Premier League and Opta Analyst, among others. He supports Wycombe Wanderers and has a soft spot for Wealdstone. A self-confessed statto, he has been known to watch football with a spreadsheet (or several) open...

#871. John Motson’s legendary voice resurrected by AI for EA FC 27

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

EA Sports said they worked with John Motson’s family to bring back his iconic voice in a ‘digital tribute’

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Legendary football commentator John Motson‘s voice is set to return to EA FC 27 through the use of AI - three years after his death.

Motson, who died aged 77 in 2023, worked on the BBC’s flagship Match of the Day programme since 1971 and covered more than 2,000 televised games, including 29 FA Cup finals and 10 World Cups.

He retired from live commentary in 2008 but continued to work on Match of the Day programme until he hung up the microphone in 2018.

EA Sports said they worked with John Motson’s family to bring back his iconic voice in a “digital tribute” through the use of new AI-tools, “bringing a mix of both his original audio and an AI-recreation trained by recordings of the man himself”.

The commentator featured in EA Sports’ annual FIFA game series from 1996 to 2006.

A studio spokesperson said EA Sports have “worked with extensive care and respect to create a digital tribute to one of the game’s greatest voices, inspiring a whole new generation of football fans.”

“My father adored being the voice of the game, and we are so grateful to the team at EA SPORTS FC for this touching tribute and preserving his memory in-game,” said Fred Motson, son of John Motson.

“His voice inspired millions of players across generations every time they picked up a controller, and now a whole new set of fans will get to experience his legacy and commentary.”

After starting as a newspaper reporter in Barnet and at the Sheffield Morning Telegraph, Motson joined the BBC in 1968 as a sports presenter on Radio 2.

His long career also took in two Olympic Games and Wimbledon’s memorable 1988 FA Cup final triumph against Liverpool at Wembley, as the Crazy Gang beat the Culture Club.

Awarded the OBE in 2001 for services to broadcasting, Motson hung up his microphone for the BBC at the end of the 2017-18 Premier League season.

EA Sports football game series began in 1994 with the release of FIFA International Soccer, with the FIFA name continuing until 2023, when the termination of EA and FIFA’s licensing agreement led to the 2024 game being called FC.

John Motson’s voice will be added to EA FC 27 in Title Update v1.3.0 on 26 November as an optional commentary selection.

#869. What are fossil fuels?

They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

#868. Spain thought it had the 2030 World Cup final. Morocco and Infantino have other plans

The contest is now tied to FIFA President Gianni Infantino's survival battle and political tensions over migration

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

When Spain secured a joint bid for the 2030 World Cup, many automatically assumed as a certainty that the final match would take place on home turf.

As former world champions – a title since won again – and the second-most visited country globally, Spain held the sporting pedigree and tourism capacity for huge crowds, creating a widespread expectation the final was guaranteed.

Co-host Portugal had no desire for the fixture, and Spanish representatives assumed Morocco, having joined the bid late, would not fight to secure it.

In recent months, however, alarm has spread across Spain that the North African nation, a rising power in world football, might steal the tournament's biggest showpiece event.

The rivalry to host the game has evolved into a fierce clash involving Real Madrid's Bernabeu, Barcelona's Camp Nou and the $1 billion Hassan II stadium now being built near legendary Casablanca.

The contest is now tied to FIFA President Gianni Infantino's survival battle and political tensions between Spain and Morocco regarding migration.

Internal politics in Spain have also been impacted, with Alberto Núñez Feijóo, frontrunner to become prime minister following Sunday's vote, insisting Spain should drop out of hosting the tournament if denied the final.

Top-flight LaLiga chief Javier Tebas and conservative mayor of Madrid José Luis Martínez-Almeida have voiced similar concerns, with the latter admitting he "wasn't optimistic" given he saw no sign that the Spanish government was matching Morocco's ambition.

Inspectors from world governing body FIFA are touring host cities during this month and next, but no date has been set for choosing the location. For the 2026 World Cup final, the venue near New York was named two years beforehand.

With its team bankrolled by ⁠the state fertilizer behemoth, Morocco has united behind bringing the final to its new stadium, named after its former king, which with a 115,000-seat capacity will ​be the world's ⁠largest soccer arena.

By contrast, Spain's campaign is divided along familiar lines between Madrid and Barcelona and their two biggest clubs.

Morocco deserves the final as much as Spain, fan Bilal Jouhari, 39, said in Rabat, pointing out that Morocco is fifth in FIFA's world rankings.

"Those who threaten to walk out if FIFA chooses Morocco as the final's host are just like those who abandon the game because they don't like the referee's decisions," said Jouhari, who runs a platform promoting cultural events.

Ricardo Trade, former CEO of the ⁠FIFA World Cup Organising Committee for Brazil 2014, said Spain should have settled which city got the final as part of the original bid.

"Spain is terrified of losing the final, a final they were absolutely certain they’d be hosting," said Trade, also CEO ​for the 2016 Olympics and deputy ⁠CEO for operations at the 2022 World Cup.

"You have Barcelona on one side saying what they want, ‌and Real Madrid on the other also saying what they want, whilst Morocco seems to be very united on this World Cup project and has a stadium for 115,000 people."

After Barcelona's president, Joan Laporta, lobbied in September for the final to go to the Camp Nou, arguing that the Bernabeu had already hosted the 1982 final, some sources in the Spanish football federation (RFEF) expressed frustration at him for undermining the unity needed to counter Morocco.

A senior Portuguese official involved in the bidding process said Spain was caught off guard, wrongly assuming that since Morocco was ‌not part of the original bid then the final was guaranteed for Spain. "They should have seen it coming," the person said.

Alvaro de Miguel, the RFEF secretary general, denied ‌there were divisions in the Spanish camp and said presenting two options against Morocco's one gave Spain better odds of success.

He noted that the bid to host the tournament was put together during a moment of instability at the Spanish FA when former president Luis Rubiales was embroiled in scandal over kissing player Jenni Hermoso on the lips at the 2023 Women's World Cup.

The atmosphere at the RFEF at the time "was not the most conducive to a project of this scale, involving a range of complex interests," he said.

It also coincided with a testy time between Spain and Morocco over migration, including a 2021 attempt by thousands of people to enter Spain's African enclave of Ceuta.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez overruled the RFEF's plans to announce ⁠the invitation to Morocco to join the bid, insisting on delivering the message himself during a bilateral visit to Rabat in 2018, according to an RFEF source.

His government was heavily involved in the creation of the bid and the RFEF ended up agreeing to a request from the government and FIFA to include Casablanca as an option for the final, according to three RFEF sources.

FIFA's Infantino has been locked in a power struggle with UEFA since Europe's governing football body demanded he step down over his plan to sell a 20% stake in the World Cup.

Tebas said Infantino would favour Morocco because it was backing his reelection bid. "If Infantino stays on, Spain’s chances of getting that final are negligible or non-existent," Tebas said in September.

Morocco's football association has been one of his staunchest supporters and Infantino has spent long periods at FIFA's newly opened regional headquarters in Rabat since the selloff plan was revealed. Infantino is the favourite to win reelection at FIFA's March congress – in Morocco.

However, Real Madrid President Florentino Perez, who has a close relationship with Infantino, could help persuade him to choose Spain for the final, a LaLiga source said.

De Miguel said the fact that FIFA's governance was under such scrutiny played in Spain's favour, since he expected it to be awarded to the "natural" candidate.

FIFA said in a statement it has no standard procedure for selecting the venue and that the decision would follow consultations with ‌host cities, countries and governments.

Spanish officials say Madrid has experience in handling high-octane matches such as the 2018 final of South America's Copa Libertadores between River Plate and Boca Juniors, switched there due to fan violence.

They also point to the debacle in ​Rabat during the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final, when Senegal's coach ordered his players off the pitch over a penalty awarded to Morocco, footballers fought each other, and the ball boys stole the Senegal goalkeeper's equipment.

De Miguel said that if size ‌is a factor, then the Camp Nou will hold 105,000 by the 2028-2029 season after a $2 billion refurbishment, compared to the ⁠Bernabeu's 84,000 after its $1.5 billion makeover.

Moroccan FA President Fouzi Lekjaa said construction of the Hassan II will be completed in early 2028. According to the IMF, Morocco plans to spend about $19 billion between 2024 and 2030 building airports, stadiums, hotels and a high-speed ⁠rail network, as well as a train station and highway to connect the stadium with Casablanca 45 km (28 miles) away.

Casablanca will need to work on its hotels to compete with Madrid and Barcelona after a FIFA technical report rated its accommodation offering for the general public at 3.1 compared to 5 for Spain.

But a successful bid is not just about who has ‌the best stadium, hotels and transport. Often bids go to the country that would ​receive the greater benefit, Trade said.

In Morocco, the World Cup was an opportunity to expand railways and develop the whole Casablanca area, Lekjaa told state ‌broadcaster 2M. A Moroccan source familiar with the discussions said the final should go to the stadium with the largest ​capacity — and to an African country.

"It would be awkward – embarrassing, even – and would send the wrong message to Africa, one of the world's biggest producers of raw football talent, if the World Cup final were ultimately awarded to a non-African country with a smaller stadium," the person said.

Large regions of chromosomes are organized into a state known as heterochromatin. This densely packed form of DNA represses gene activity. Curiously, some families of clustered genes can be activated even though they are packed as heterochromatin. Writing in Nature, Buckley et al.1 report findings that explain this paradox: they show how opposing mechanisms that control the organization of heterochromatin promote the stochastic activation of genes in the protocadherin (Pcdh) gene cluster, thereby supporting proper nervous-system development.

Manchester United's No.1 was dependable last season - but hasn't seemed himself this term

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There were other factors that led to Manchester United’s 4-0 defeat to Liverpool besides Senne Lammens’ performance, like Leny Yoro’s red card after only eight minutes. Down to 10 men for the majority of the match, Mauricio Pochettino’s debut as manager became about damage limitation from that point on.

And yet in the post-match analysis, Manchester United’s first-choice goalkeeper still found himself scrutinised. “If he’s in the right position, he saves it comfortably,” argued Danny Murphy on Match of the Day, highlighting Lammens’ positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opener.

It wasn’t the first time a Lammens mistake has been highlighted this season. While the Belgian was widely hailed for his performances in his debut Premier League campaign after joining from Royal Antwerp, the malaise around him at Old Trafford has dragged him down. He, like many of his United teammates, is under-performing.

Before the November international break, Lammens was blamed for two goals in the chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, too easily beaten at his near post by Alysson for Villa’s first and spilling a shot for Nicolas Jackson to make it 2-0 after only four minutes. He was shaky throughout.

There was also Lammens’ ill-judged decision to come rushing off his line against Bournemouth, giving Evanilson the chance to finish into an empty net in a 3-0 win for the Cherries at Old Trafford. The messy own goal conceded by Manchester United in the 1-1 draw away to Fulham was another that involved Lammens.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence. His struggles can be traced back to the World Cup where he made a blunder that led to Belgium’s exit from the tournament, spilling a shot for Mikel Merino to score a late winner for Spain. Lammens hasn’t been the same since that moment.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There are, however, some mitigating factors to explain the goalkeeper’s form. For starters, Lammens is having to make more saves this season. Last season, the 24-year-old averaged 2.4 saves per 90 minutes in the Premier League, whereas this season that number has increased to 3.6 saves per 90 minutes.

Only Crystal Palace have conceded more Expected Goals (xG) in the Premier League this season than Manchester United. Lammens is being afforded very little protection by the players in front of him, as demonstrated by United’s shambolic defensive performance at Anfield on Sunday.

For comparison, Manchester United conceded the fourth-lowest xG over the course of the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Their sudden defensive drop-off is somewhat unexplainable, but it goes a long way to reasoning why Lammens is struggling so much. He’s simply having to do more. He’s being overwhelmed.

Lammens hasn’t actually regressed much in terms of his save percentage. This season, the Belgian is ranked 16th in the Premier League for this metric, whereas last season he was 14th. Lammens has never been anywhere near the most effective shot-stoppers in this regard.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence

It’s possible Lammens over-performed last season. Without the Belgian settling so quickly after arriving as an emergency upgrade on Andre Onana and Altay Bayindir, it’s difficult to envisage Manchester United finishing third. His saves did a lot to mask some of United’s structural deficiencies.

No goalkeeper in the Premier League last season prevented more goals than Lammens (6.4). That ranked him ahead of the likes of Gianluigi Donnarumma, Emi Martinez, Jordan Pickford, Alisson Becker and David Raya. It was perhaps unrealistic to expect someone still so young in goalkeeper years to maintain such a high level.

“This break came at the ideal moment for me,” said Lammens in the last international break during which he played the full 90 minutes in back-to-back games for Belgium against Turkey and Italy, saving a penalty against the latter. “These have been difficult weeks for me at Manchester United.”

Life for Lammens didn’t get any easier in his first match back from international duty, although the Belgian’s seven saves prevented the scoreline from being even more humiliating for Manchester United. There were moments when Lammens showed the sort of form that made him so eye-catching last season.

Pochettino might find a way to steady Manchester United at the back. The Argentine set up the Old Trafford outfit with a back three in possession before Yoro’s red card completely changed the dynamic of the match. With 11 men on the pitch, Pochettino should find it easier to implement a defensive game plan, although that’s something Michael Carrick never managed.

This could help Lammens rediscover his best form. If not, Manchester United will need their goalkeeper to eliminate the errors from his performances on his own accord, otherwise a relegation scrap at the bottom of the Premier League table could be unavoidable. Lammens can’t count on getting any more help any time soon.

#865. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

#864. Doctor who helped save Fabrice Muamba struck off after relationship with ‘vulnerable’ patient

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Jonathan Tobin helped Fabrice Muamba after he collapsed on the pitch during an FA Cup match in March 2012

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A medical tribunal has heard that a doctor who helped save the life of Premier League footballer Fabrice Muamba engaged in sexual activity with a "vulnerable" patient on practice premises during working hours.

Dr Jonathan Tobin, based at Kirkham Health Centre in Preston, was among four men who assisted Muamba when the midfielder suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch while playing for Bolton at Tottenham in an FA Cup match in March 2012.

Muamba’s heart stopped for 78 minutes, but he was able to make a full recovery before announcing his retirement from football five months after the incident.

Mr Tobin received further praise in November 2021 when Wigan Athletic striker Charlie Wyke thanked him for saving his life following a cardiac arrest during training.

However, Mr Tobin has now been struck off the medical register after scheduling unnecessary medical appointments to meet a "vulnerable" woman and subsequently falsifying her medical records to cover up their relationship, a Medical Practitioners Tribunal panel wrote.

The panel heard that their relationship initiated after they kissed inside his consulting room in July 2024 and persisted until November of that year. Mr Tobin admitted to engaging in sexual activity at the surgery during working hours, and acknowledged dishonestly altering her records twice to state she failed to attend appointments.

Fully aware of the woman’s vulnerability, Mr Tobin acknowledged that she needed "a good empathic GP", adding: "What she got was incredibly harmful." Stephen Brassington, his legal representative, stated that the doctor accepted complete responsibility, noting that his shame and contrition "could not be more obvious".

The tribunal observed that Mr Tobin’s professional style was "informal, friendly, and made use of humour", adding: "He enjoyed being popular with his patients, rather than being formal."

The panel further wrote: "Dr Tobin allowed himself to form a sexual relationship with this patient in his surgery when all his professional training and experience will have told him that behaviour of that nature was unacceptable."

Despite acknowledging that Mr Tobin had been a "fine doctor", the panel concluded that maintaining his registration would undermine public trust and confidence in the profession, issuing an immediate order of suspension.
