#809. 'Holes in the system' - LET star wants more pathways to earn LPGA cards

Casandra Alexander has won the Ladies European Tour Order of Merit after three wins and five runner-up finishes in 2026; Alexander secured her LPGA Tour card via Q-Series ahead of the season-ending Andalucía Costa del Sol Open de Espana, live on Sky Sports Golf

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Ladies European Tour Order of Merit winner Casandra Alexander has called for more pathways to be introduced to avoid players being ‘stuck’ in the same way she was to secure her LPGA Tour card.

Alexander is inside the world's top 30, has won three times on the Ladies European Tour this season and wrapped up the Order of Merit title with two events to spare, yet still needed to negotiate Final Qualifying to secure her LPGA Tour card for next season.

The South African has been a dominant force on the LET this season, posting five runner-up finishes before following KPMG Women's Irish Open victory with further wins at the Buccellati Ladies Italian Open and Wistron Ladies Open.

PGA Tour membership is offered in the men's game via the DP World Tour's Race to Dubai rankings, with the top 10 - not already exempt - earning their card this season, whereas top LET performers still need to earn LPGA cards via their Q-Series.

"It's definitely a little disappointing," Alexander admitted to Sky Sports. "There's not one person to blame - there's structures in place and I think it just shows the holes in the structure that we need to change.

"There's a lot that goes into it, but it was also a proving point for me this year, to get my world ranking as high as possible. I was hoping to break into the top 20 and go 'really, guys, are we still going to say there's only one way to get a card and that's Q-School?'

"We need to fix the system and we need to work together, because we want the best players in the world playing against the best players in the world and all having that opportunity."

Alexander enters the season-ending Andalucía Costa del Sol Open de Espana without a practice round having safely negotiated LPGA Qualifying, finishing Monday, where a final-round 64 helped secure her card on the American circuit next season.

"I'm not saying we need to hand out [LPGA] cards, but there surely has to be more than one pathway to earn it?" Alexander added. "I don't think the point of it is to say, 'oh, look at this, it's absolute rubbish', which it is, it's going, 'cool, but how do we do better?'

"I'm sure I wouldn't have the same attitude if I didn't get my card. I went there, I got my card, but how do we do better for the next people coming through? Because this isn't going to sustain itself - you're going to lose great players over this.

"A lot say the top three or top five on the LET Order of Merit should get cards - that's not necessarily how it starts. I think the conversation starts around 'how do I play my way into LPGA events, into gaining points and into potentially getting a full card?'

"It also shows that we need to be line-up with world ranking points because I don't understand how I was 23rd in the world and could play every major but couldn't play a general LPGA Tour event - that shows another hole in the system.

"We need to have a 'top 100 in the world' spot for any LPGA event. We have that on the LET and that would have given me opportunity to play eight or nine LPGA events this year. I hope someone else doesn't get stuck in the same situation I did in the future."

Alexander was keen to taper expectations heading into the season finale, given she only arrived in Spain the day before the tournament and without her luggage, although she is keen to enjoy the experience and celebrate an impressive season.

"I felt a little lighter leaving Alabama with the [LPGA Tour] card in my hands," Alexander admitted. "We're just coming in this week to have fun. We'll give it our best and I think it's important to show face as winner of the Order of Merit at the final event - that shows a lot of character.

"I'd love to be at home celebrating but, at the same time, it's going to be a fun week. There's the award ceremony afterwards and I think now I can take it all in. We've got a lot to do and a lot to plan [for 2027], and it's very exciting.

"It has been a really big, successful year. A lot learned and I have a great team around me that I can be thankful for, for all these achievements. It's a bit surreal, but still so much I want to do."

#808. Wolf Biermann at 90: The singer who defied East Germany

His life is a reflection of contemporary German history, addressed via his songs and sharp wit. At 90, he's as feisty as ever.

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's new album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann has said his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama."

Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism."

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann said. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer."

In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. "

I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he said.

He became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he said. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom."

The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he said, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

And should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

This article was originally written in German.

#807. Why are there 2:05pm kick-offs in the Premier League on Sunday?

Everton's derby with Liverpool has been moved from Saturday to Sunday

The Premier League kick-off times look a little unusual this weekend, with no Saturday 12:30 GMT slot, and games starting at 12:00 and 14:05 on Sunday.

Everton will host local rivals Liverpool on Sunday at 12 noon because the match has been selected for live broadcast by TNT, who have a mid-day broadcast slot on that day. The game was originally scheduled for Saturday.

This has had a knock-on effect on the remaining fixtures.

On a typical Premier League weekend, the first matches will begin at 14:00 followed by a final 16:30 kick-off.

Pushing start times back five minutes to 14:05 reduces the risk of overlap with the unusual early 12:00 start time, while avoiding clashing with the 16:30 fixture.

Midweek European games have also affected the schedule, as the Premier League aims to prevent clubs from playing two matches within 60 hours of each other.

Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Bournemouth and Brighton are all set to play in the Europa and Conference Leagues on Thursday, ruling them out of Saturday Premier League fixtures.

#803. Ukraine: Zelenskyy says security deal could go to referendum

The US has broached the idea of Kyiv giving up the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, the Ukrainian president said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US peace envoys asked whether Kyiv would withdraw from its eastern region of ‌Donbas ⁠in exchange ⁠for joining NATO, according to remarks to the media published on Saturday.

The suggestion was made following the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi to bring Russia's nearly 5-year war in Ukraine to a close.

The Ukrainian leader told reporters: "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would ⁠Ukraine ​withdraw from Donbas?'"

Zelenskyy repeated Kyiv's position that it was not willing to cede territory to Russia. But he added that if the country reached a comprehensive deal, including security guarantees, a ‌strong ​and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question ​to the public in a referendum.

"That ​is why ⁠I believe NATO is back on the ⁠agenda. ​But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Zelenskyy said the prospect of NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas has not been raised before.

He also warned about Moscow's plan to  change the continent's security architecture, saying it could lead to more conflict.

Putin has demanded that NATO pull back its troops from the Russian border, which European Union leaders have strongly criticized.

"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelenskyy added.

"Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Friday, the EU said several European diplomats would take part in future Ukraine peace talks, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland.

Moscow has long insisted that European states be excluded from the negotiations because they support Ukraine.

The comments come as Russia’s Defence Ministry said its ⁠forces ⁠had captured the ​settlement of Tersianka in ​Ukraine’s southeastern ​Zaporizhzhia ‌region, news agency Interfax reported.

Interfax cited the ministry as saying that Russian ​forces had struck Ukrainian energy and ​transport infrastructure used by ⁠the ​military, along with ammunition ​depots and ​drone production ‌and storage sites.

Russia has targeted power stations across Ukraine in waves of ballistic and cruise missile attacks, cutting power and heating to millions of people as temperatures plunge.

Zelenskyy warned that Putin was "betting everything" on this winter's war campaign, which Kyiv insists is aimed at hurting public morale.

#802. Do Ferrari need to make Hamilton their No 1 driver?

Listen to the latest edition of The F1 Show podcast as Simon Lazenby, David Croft and Jamie Chadwick debate what's next at Ferrari after another driver clash; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton's latest run-in at the Las Vegas Grand Prix has ramped up scrutiny on Ferrari and what the team will do to try to avoid more costly on-track incidents between their two drivers.

Just two races after a fierce battle when running first and second on the opening lap in Mexico City cost the team victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen and led to clear-the-air discussions, the team-mates collided when battling over sixth place in Las Vegas in an incident Leclerc was found at fault for by the stewards and then received the post-race ire of team boss Frederic Vasseur.

Vasseur has said such incidents "cannot continue" but how does the Frenchman get on top of the situation heading towards 2027, when the team will be hoping to launch a fresh bid to end what stands as an 18-year world title drought?

The Ferrari fallout proved a central topic on the latest edition of Sky Sports' The F1 Show podcast ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, in which host Simon Lazenby was joined by David Croft and Jamie Chadwick.

Asked how big the problems between Hamilton and Leclerc were becoming for Ferrari, Chadwick said: "Significant when you think about what they're going to potentially be going into next year with.

"I think this is the time of the year where you don't want to be having these kinds of conflicts because suddenly it will escalate and it will mean that more serious conversation is going to be had in the background."

Former world champion Damon Hill recently said he believed Ferrari should make Hamilton, the seven-time world champion and F1's most successful driver, their clear No 1 next year if they want to win the world championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Speaking on Sky Sports F1 after Sunday's incident in Las Vegas, Jacques Villeneuve, the 1997 title winner, suggested Leclerc - who is in his eighth season with the Scuderia - had "lost" the leadership of the team to Hamilton, who is in his second, and "if there's one of the two drivers knows how to win championships, it's Lewis".

Villeneuve did, however, question whether Ferrari would be able to prioritise Hamilton contractually.

Hamilton said after the race that he has "never asked" for No 1 status at the team, although implied they could have given him more backing when he was second to Kimi Antonelli and around 40 points ahead of Leclerc in the championship earlier this season.

And although Hamilton and Leclerc are both among the sport's biggest names and most-talented drivers, Croft believes events of this season have effectively forced the team's hand and they need to prioritise one over the other in order to achieve better results.

"Whether Lewis Hamilton is asking to be No 1 or not, I don't think matters any more," said Croft.

"I think the way things have panned out this season the matter has been forced.

"Lewis has to be the No 1 because Charles keeps putting himself in a position whereby Ferrari suffer when the two drivers come together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"He got the penalty on Sunday. Whether you think it's a penalty or not, the move was ambitious and it was ambitious if it was a move on Lando Norris, it was ambitious and a bit foolish if it's a move on your own team-mate.

"So Charles is kind of forcing, albeit not deliberately, Ferrari to make these decisions. He did race Lewis hard in Mexico City, and we saw what happened there, and he raced Lewis hard in Monza, and we saw what happened there."

Long regarded as one of the fastest drivers in the sport, Leclerc, 29, is a graduate of Ferrari's academy and joined their race team in 2019 after a debut season of F1 at Sauber.

He outperformed four-time champion Sebastian Vettel and then Carlos Sainz across their respective seasons as team-mates and was comfortably ahead of Hamilton by over 80 points after the Briton joined from Mercedes last year.

But Leclerc has faced a resurgent force in Hamilton this year, with the 41-year-old holding a 17-point advantage over him in the championship with two races to go.

"Charles is a fine driver, don't get me wrong, but his pole-to-win conversion rate (27 to nine) is not enough," added Croft on Leclerc's Ferrari record so far.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"You can also argue that the team haven't given him the car to make that conversion rate better, but he does make mistakes, we've seen that.

"We've seen in the past when he's been leading a race and he's crashed out all by himself. He's not the finished article and I don't want to be too harsh on Charles because I think he's a truly wonderful human being, but he's no Lewis Hamilton when it comes to his record and his performances and his consistency over the years."

Vasseur said he would hold fresh discussions with his drivers this week.

But do those talks need to now go further in terms of setting out firmly what is and is not acceptable - and establishing consequences for any transgressions?

Chadwick said: "I think the biggest issue [to this point] is the conversations haven't been serious enough.

"I think a clear-the-air talk as in 'okay it's not your fault, it's not your fault' and 'okay this is how things are' versus, actually, what are the rules of engagement? What are the reprimands if you do take your team-mate out and are they severe enough that actually neither driver is going to dare put themselves in that position?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Clearly not because when you look at the move Charles did. Okay I kind of agree a little bit it wasn't not on, but it's definitely not on on your team-mate. I think you can maybe risk a move like Lando did on Lewis and I think that's also actually where Charles was a bit unlucky [in that he] went for it and then he kind of sees the door closing a bit and then he backs out and then it's kind of worse because he's over the kerb and that's what caused him to hit him.

"If he had actually just really committed to it maybe it would have been a bit better but, either way, you just never do that on your team-mate and clearly he didn't see there being any risk as to making a move like that on his team-mate. In his mind in that moment, Lewis is the same as any other driver on that grid. it's not a car in the same team as you.

"So that definitely needs a lot of discussion behind the scenes."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chadwick, though, believes it is possible to win world titles with two No 1 drivers.

"I think it can still work with two drivers of top calibre but there has to be clear rules of engagement," she added.

"That's what we were arguably critical of, but it worked for McLaren last year."

But given the repeat nature of the on-track clashes and flashpoints between Hamilton and Leclerc this season, Croft is unsure much will actually change despite the incident and another round of discussions.

"They either say 'Lewis is No 1 going forward' and 'sorry, Charles, you're not going to get involved with this and you're going to drive for your team-mate because we need a championship here'. Or they get a new team principal who can actually maybe have a better sway over the two drivers, because at the moment it looks like whatever Fred says it just gets ignored out on track. Or they can just carry on as they are doing.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"And if I was going to put whatever dollars you had left over from Vegas on this one, I'd probably say Ferrari are just going to carry on and do what they did this year next year as well because they've had every chance so far this year to actually address the situation and they've not addressed it right so far."

#801. The best European strikers this century - ranked by you

The top 10 European strikers of the 21st century

Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.

There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.

This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.

Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.

We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.

So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.

Top 10 European Strikers of the Century - Part One

Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.

Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'."

Honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player."

Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.

The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.

Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher."

Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries."

Zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.

Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think."

Laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible."

Honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that."

The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.

Honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi."

Balague: "What could have been, yes. He was the national team's record scorer too before Harry Kane took it. I find him to deserve this place as he had to adapt to a lot of strikers and he did it well. He had the ability to link up and score. He was very intelligent."

Laurens: "He is the most street footballer England has ever seen. There's no rules, that kind of anger you saw on the pitch. I don't think people in England realise how good he was."

What does becoming the all-time World Cup top goalscorer get you? Sixth place on the best European strikers this century list. The Real Madrid forward, 27, just misses out on the top five.

Laurens: "Maybe if we do this ranking again in a few years he will be higher. I would have had him top five, for sure. He has scored more than 400 goals. I don't think Messi and Ronaldo had scored that many at that age, so he's ahead. I don't know if he will play for as long as them but he hasn't done much wrong in his career."

Balague: "This list has to do what you feel about the player, not science - 22 goals in 22 appearances in World Cups and [Euro] Championships. He should be at least top three because of that. Great stats, but we're not in love with him."

Honigstein: "I don't think there is a forward that is as good as footballer as him in 2026. On that basis alone he should be higher, but people when they vote have other things in their head. The only way to win everyone over is to score more goals and win more World Cups for France, which I think is possible."

There was little between Mbappe and Erling Haaland, but it is Manchester City's prolific Norwegian who slips in at fifth. The 26-year-old has already scored more than 300 club goals and has a staggering 68 in 61 games for his country.

Balague: "Mbappe should be higher than him. Haaland scored 52 goals in 53 games [in 2022-23], that is astonishing, but he's gone 11 finals without scoring. We're talking about the best. We're talking about what we see at the moment and what we see is someone who is calculated but in a more charming way. An ability to score we haven't seen in a while; power, ability to finish. He is not world class to the level of others."

Honigstein: "I don't think it's fair to judge him on just that. They [Manchester City] won the Champions League when he was there. When Haaland arrived with Pep Guardiola, they found a way to do it. What makes him unique is the physical attributes and the pace. To have both is unique. He can sprint like a 100m sprinter. Is he the fifth best striker of the 21st Century? I don't think he's that far behind."

Interesting, this, because Robert Lewandowski is well clear of Haaland in fourth, but the leap from the Polish forward to the top three is massive - more than 10,000 votes.

The 38-year-old is still chipping away for Chicago Fire in Major League Soccer, having been a reliably ruthless assassin for Barcelona, Bayern and Dortmund.

Honigstein: "He used to play basketball, judo, handball - his father wanted him to have a wholesome education. You could see his completeness that he had as a centre-forward. Nothing in his game was extraordinary but in terms of ticking all the boxes, none come close to him."

Balague: "He said he learned to be an elite striker when he forgot what he had just done, like a fish. Mistakes he had in his head affected his performance. One day he just continued like it didn't matter."

Laurens: "He won the Ballon d'Or in Covid, it won't be on his mantlepiece but we all know it was his."

Fresh from his Ballon d'Or triumph, England's record goalscorer and appearance maker rides into the top three on the back of 61 goals in 51 outings for Bayern Munich last season.

Kane left the Premier League three years ago with the second-most goals ever in the competition, and is also Tottenham's all-time record scorer.

Honigstein: "Third place, at least. He is doing incredible things. At 33, still not quite at his peak. I don't think he relies on his pace, physicality, it's all about intelligence, technique. I don't think there's anyone in the game that strikes a ball as well as him right now. I don't think any player comes close that we've talked about so far in overall work-rate, defending, helping the team, making tackles in your box in the 90th minute when you're 3-0 up because he's that kind of guy. He is humble and a superb human being."

Laurens: "What I love about Kane, from a young age, a lot of this list you just knew the trajectory would be all the way to the top. Kane was not like that. It could have been very different for him. Nobody at 17 would've said he was going to win the Ballon d'Or. Nobody believed in him like the others. Kane had a very different journey."

Runner-up Thierry Henry is the only striker in the top six who is retired. A World Cup and Euros winner with France, Henry won titles with Arsenal - where he scored 228 goals - and a Champions League with Barcelona.

Honigstein: "During his time, I don't think there was a player like him in the Premier League. The way he played football was stylish, elegant, but there was almost a kind of a romantic connection between him and the ball. I don't think there was anyone near that kind of level of technique and, for want of a better word, va-va-voom he exuded. That just made for amazing viewing."

Laurens: "For me as a fellow Parisien, he's a very special player, a very special man. A career that has been incredible from a young age. It's that season in the Premier League - 24 goals, 20 assists in 38 games - not even Kane or Benzema or Cristiano, OK, Messi is different, but they haven't done that and yet he did it.

"There are still some people who undervalue him and underappreciate him and the monster that he was on the football pitch. He had it all. The pace, the style, the elegance, the technique, the mentality, the goals, the aura, the charisma. Just everything you wanted if you were to build a striker. One of the greatest football brains ever."

Of course, at number one, it's the man chasing the 1,000-goal dream. Cristiano Ronaldo may have retired from Portugal duty with 146 notches on his strike chart but the quest goes on at Al-Nassr.

The 41-year-old's evolution from tricky winger to prolific frontman has taken him from Sporting to Manchester United, twice, Real Madrid, Juventus and now Saudi Arabia.

Balague: "He's the best striker in history. His numbers are incredible. He won't stop until he gets to 1,000. He is somebody who is special. We know his background, how he wanted to be Ballon d'Or winner at 12 and didn't stop until he got there. He ran up the mountains of Funchal with weights in his ankles and snuck into the gym when it was closed to get the physique he wanted."

Laurens: "Always in the right place at the right time. The instinct. He was born with a gift, like all in this list. But you still have to work hard. Nobody will ever reach those levels again. 1,000 goals for club and country will never be done again, I think."

Honigstein: "Peak Ronaldo for me was Gareth Bale scoring and him looking very unhappy. I don't think there will be any dispute about him being the greatest. Somebody who has done it all, won it all, and he's still going for the love of it."

#800. How Premier League's big six keep getting richer

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by Â£85m.

"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.

"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."

The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m."

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.

The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

#799. Walters confident he can win trophy in first season with St Helens

New St Helens coach Kevin Walters has pinpointed where he believes things may have gone wrong for the club in 2026; St Helens missed the Super League play-offs for the first time in the club's history; Walters put pen to paper on a three-year deal in August

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Kevin Walters believes he can win a trophy with St Helens in his first season in charge, as the side's new head coach set out his ambition to restore the team's "winning DNA".

After guiding Australia to their fourth consecutive Rugby League World Cup success earlier this month, the former Brisbane Broncos boss has been tasked with galvanising the Saints following an underwhelming season that saw them slump to seventh in Super League and miss the play-offs for the first time in the club's history.

The 59-year-old, who put pen to paper on a three-year deal with the Saints in August, is confident he can restore the club to where it belongs and added St Helens are "not in as bad a position as some people may think".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Asked by Sky Sports Rugby League's Jenna Brooks whether he can win silverware in his first season, Walters said: "If I say no to that question, I look like a loser. I'm not a loser. I love winning.

"So I'm going to answer that positively and say yeah, I believe we can have great success here.

"It starts early; the pressure is on. I've been at big clubs and I understand the pressure that comes with it. I understand there's a lot of pressure on myself and the club to do well. But I'm confident we can do really well.

"Pressure is a privilege, isn't it? I wouldn't be in the role if I didn't [have that] understanding. There's always pressure in professional sport, particularly in rugby league - in Australia and here in the Super League. It's a big sport in the north.

"Everyone knows about St Helens and their success, and we need to get them back to where they belong."

It was a turbulent season for the 10-time Super League Grand Final winners, who suffered a swathe of injuries to key players, including Matty Lees and Jack Welsby, which contributed to their disappointing form.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

St Helens also underwent some major coaching upheavals, with head coach Paul Rowley departing in May, less than a year into his three-year contract, before Eamon O'Carroll took over on an interim basis.

Club chiefs then turned to Walters, one of rugby league's most distinguished coaches. It will mark the first time the 59-year-old has taken up a full-time coaching role since he was sacked by the Brisbane Broncos in September 2024.

Walters, who arrived in the United Kingdom on Monday and has already led a few training sessions with his new team, pinpoints a loss of connection between his players and fans as one of the side's biggest issues.

"It's hard to judge from afar. I've been speaking to people in the club; the connection between the team and the community is one thing that has been lost a little bit," Walters said.

"The Saints fans, from what I've seen and been told, are very passionate about their club. The English fans, across all of the teams, their passion is a little bit different to the Australian fans, who are probably not as vocal in their support, but also in their care for the side.

"I know there were some things that did go wrong; maybe the connection among the players was lost a little bit as well."

Walters, who also spearheaded Melbourne Storm's 2012 NRL Grand Final win, and won back-to-back State of Origin series as Queensland head coach in 2016 and 2017, believes he is the right man to solve that connectivity issue.

"One of my great strengths as a coach is my ability to bring people together for a common cause, and that's what I feel coaching is. Lots of things go into coaching; my ability to bring players and teams together, that's where I feel my big strength is.

"If I can do that here… well, I will do that here and then we'll see where that takes us."

He added: "Without making too many bold predictions, we're going to be hard to beat. That's the mainstay for me. Defensively, we've spoken to our players about getting better in that space.

"The last time Saints won the premiership in 2022, it was based on defence. We have to make sure we have a strong defensive team that's well connected and then when we get the ball, we're going to play some footy.

"The best defensive teams are there where it matters."

Reports have suggested that Tristan Sailor is being eyed up as a potential target for multiple other Super League clubs.

The full-back, who previously played under Walters at the Broncos, joined the Saints in August 2024 and has gone on to make 54 appearances for the club.

While Welsby is favoured to lock down the No 1 jumper for St Helens, Walters insisted Sailor still has a future at the club.

"There's a lot of noise around the whole group and Tristan has been caught up in that," Walters said. "I believe Tristan's got a lot to offer this club still.

"He's been a great player here. I coached him at the Broncos and unfortunately Reece Walsh was parked in front of him in that role at full-back.

"He's come here in a different role, but I feel Tristan... whatever position he plays - he was good playing full-back, centre, five-eighth, he might have played some wing. Mr Versatility but also a very good team person."

#798. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists aren't convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they said AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But Herrmann said it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," said Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

#797. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.

European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.

Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.

Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

With uncertainty over how much support Tashima will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

#796. Steven Hack, Broadway Star and American Horror Story Actor, Dead at 68

Broadway star Steven Hack—also known for roles on shows like Seinfeld, General Hospital and American Horror Story—has died at age 68.

A bright light in Hollywood has gone dim.

Broadway star Steven Hack, who also had minor roles in American Horror Story and Seinfeld, has died after suffering a medical emergency, Los Angeles’ Interact Theatre Company confirmed. He was 68.

“It is with great sadness that we share the news that Steven Hack, a founding member of Interact Theatre Company, recently passed away at home following a sudden and unexpected cardiac event,” the company wrote in a recent statement shared to Instagram. “Steven was a gifted and versatile performer, a superb graphic artist, and a cherished member of our artistic family.”

Hack died of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner, a condition caused by plaque buildup in the arterial walls, per the America Heart Association.

“His creativity and talent helped shape Interact in its earliest years,” the statement continued, “and his artistry, humor, warmth, and generous spirit enriched everything he touched.”

Hack was born in St. Louis in 1958 before going on to study at the California Institute of the Arts and the American Academy of Dramatic Arts.

“Steven took great pride in his early career as a Broadway dancer, which included performing in the original production of CATS and touring with A Chorus Line,” Interact Theatre Company noted. “Here in Los Angeles, he went on to work extensively in film, television, and commercials.”

In fact, he made his screen debut as one of the teenage dancers in the 1978 film Grease before landing roles in other films like Fantastic Four, Thor: The Dark World and The Happytime Murders.

He also dominated the small screen with credits in American Horror Story: 1984, Marvel’s Agent Carter, Criminal Minds, The Newsroom, Days of Our Lives, The West Wing, Scrubs, General Hospital, Seinfeld and so many more.

“As we remember Steven, we celebrate not only his many contributions to our company, but also the joy of knowing and working with him,” Interact Theatre Company wrote. “He will always hold a special place in Interact’s history and in the hearts of those who knew him.”

They expressed hope that Hack’s "memory be a blessing,” adding, "We extend our heartfelt condolences to his family, friends, and all who loved him.”

#795. One of football's most-hyped 16-year-olds - what next for JJ Gabriel?

JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season

It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.

Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.

Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.

His father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.

Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.

How long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.

When Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he said: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me."

In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.

Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message

Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market

For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.

Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.

It fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.

Barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.

The expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.

Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.

Madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the plan is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.

Where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.

The idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.

"Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.

Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.

Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat says he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.

After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.

His major football experience before that? The football game Championship Manager.

"I was always trading players," he told ESPN this year. "I was obsessed with every single player around the world."

This was not just about living out a fantasy in the real world. Barat was drawn into the profession because of the vast sums agents can earn in commission.

What makes his agency "boutique"? Unlike the top operations which have a huge number of players on their books, Epic Sports aims to have just 22 - two for each position.

This, Barat argues, ensures there is never any conflict of interest in how he represents his players.

Barat offers bespoke management of a player's career and came to prominence in the summer of 2025 when 15 of his players moved on.

This included Dean Huijsen joining Real Madrid, Nicolas Jackson moving to Bayern Munich and Xavi Simons signing for Tottenham Hotspur. Noni Madueke left Chelsea for Arsenal, and the Gunners signed Piero Hincapie.

This led to Barat being named Golden Boy Best Agent for the second time in three years.

Yet he is largely the figurehead, with agents working on his behalf around Europe. For instance, Epic has three other agents registered with the English Football Association (FA).

Barat, who also brokered Moises Caicedo's move to Chelsea, says he uses social media, and in particular influencer Fabrizio Romano, to amplify stories and agree transfers on his terms.

"Ali Barat redefines the game again," read an Epic Sports press release to announce Jackson's loan move to Bayern. No other agency seems to promote itself in this way.

The largely AI-generated video which announced Gabriel had joined Epic Sports was right on brand.

Gabriel's deal is part of a new venture: Epic Future - and this presents an ethical problem.

"It is about targeting the biggest young players, especially where they're not necessarily on the longest contracts," a Premier League source said. "And move them overseas for cheap fees.

"The original club will get a few 100,000 euros if that, and everyone else will hoover up millions and millions and millions - including his family."

Transferring a player to Europe also opens the door to future sell-on fees for an agent, which is against FA regulations.

It is this new focus on younger players which has started to cause friction at some top clubs.

No club wants to lose players they have spent years developing for nothing, only for an agent to reap the rewards.

Manchester United had to work hard 18 months ago to convince JJ Gabriel and his family that Old Trafford was the right place to further his football education.

The big question is, did they overpromise in doing so?

Sources close to the player eventually felt they were let down and United did not deliver on what was expected.

Certainly around Gabriel's pre-season minutes and presence in the squad for the Champions League opener against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK, which it was felt would be a perfect opportunity for the youngster to make his debut.

By the time the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton came round, there was no faith Gabriel would be brought on. Given United lost 3-2, there is merit in that stance.

The secondary elements are where will Gabriel develop the most?

United's academy is one of the best in England at producing young players, but given his size, will the forward benefit more from being in a less physical environment?

There has been a lot of sniping around his decision to leave United, but his stats are impressive and he is clearly a player of huge potential. United would certainly have wished the situation had not unfolded the way it has.

Bella Hadid is building her own slice of heaven.

The Victoria's Secret Angel, who recently hard launched her relationship with cowboy Nathan Lacy, detailed her desires to become a mom, sharing that she's ready to settle down in a quieter life.

“I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community," Hadid told Harper's Bazaar in an interview published Nov. 23. "I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother."

“It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me," she continued. "My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it."

In fact, the supermodel—who previously dated The Weeknd, art director Marc Kalman and rodeo star Adan Banuelos—views on personal success have now shifted.

“From an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion shows you do. And that is really important in our industry, especially when you’re building,” she explained. “But for me, I am different.”

That's why the 30-year-old—already aunt to sister Gigi Hadid’s daughter Khai, 6, with ex Zayn Malik—is pivoting her goals. As she put it, "Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals."

The couple also enjoyed a hockey date night at the Detroit Red Wings vs. Colorado Avalanche game, with Hadid captioning photos of herself and Lacy on Instagram Nov. 9, "Saturday night was especially meaningful."

"I’ve always loved hockey living in NYC," she added. "And being a Colorado girl at heart, growing up here since i was young, I guess it was only a matter of time before I found my way to the @coloradoavalanche. "
