#740. Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?

Manchester United are in the Premier League relegation zone 11 games into the season

Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.

Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?

While Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points last term, they actually started the season better than United have this season. After 11 games in 2025-26, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.

But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

While the table prompted talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.

United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.

But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.

While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.

Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

And it is not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.

By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the percentage chance of each club finishing in each position.

While the above means it is more likely United will survive, it is worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

There is a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.

History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.

Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.

A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.

Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.

Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there would not be entirely unprecedented.

It is a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they have played than they did last season.

Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last term.

Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.

While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals.

So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his new club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

#737. Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."

But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

#736. DWTS’ Val Chmerkovskiy Looks So Different With Hair Transformation

Val Chmerkovskiy is jiving with a new look.

The Dancing With the Stars pro appeared on the season 35 finale Nov. 24 sporting a completely new hairdo than viewers were used to.

Instead of slicking back his dark mane, Chmerkovskiy kept his hair flowing around him in a bob that swung around with his movements as he and partner Jenna Dewan—who were eliminated on the Nov. 10 episode—showed off their dance moves alongside their fellow eliminated contestants.

And it certainly took fans a minute to clock the 40-year-old when he waltzed onto the episode.

“I thought Val was Benny Blanco…,” one user wrote on Threads. Another joked, “Is that Val or Lil Dicky?”

One fan noted Chmerkovskiy also appeared to be channeling Bob Ross with his curly ‘do, sharing a photo of the famed painter with the caption, “Val tonight.”

After his elimination from DWTS, the dance pro shared how he got some much-needed encouragement from his and wife Jenna Johnson's son Rome, 3.

"It's OK to lose, right?" Chmerkovskiy asked the toddler in a Nov. 11 Instagram video, to which Rome replied, "Yeah, you try your best. If you don't win sometimes, you try to do it so many times."

And as Chmerkovskiy told his son, “You gotta learn how to do both. You gotta learn how to win. You gotta learn how to lose, and it's OK to be sad when you lose for a little bit."

Plus, he knew he was ahead of the pack having Rome in his corner, telling his son, “Even though I lost and I'm sad, I feel already better because I have you in my life."

#735. Leicester no longer for sale as owner looks to future

King Power, the Thai business that Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha is part of, bought Leicester for Â£35m in 2010

Leicester City owner Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha has confirmed the one-time Premier League title winners are no longer up for sale and there will be a "refocus" on rebuilding the side after years of decline.

The Foxes were put on the market in the summer after back-to-back relegations saw the side drop from the Premier League and straight through the Championship to land in England's third tier for just the second time in the club's 142-year history.

A sales brochure was produced by US investment bank Citigroup in which an asking price of more than Â£200m was put on a League One club that a decade ago had defied all expectations by winning the Premier League title at 5,000-1 odds.

Leicester never publicly acknowledged that the club had been put up for sale, with under-fire chief football officer Jon Rudkin going so far as to say he "cannot comment on speculation" when asked about it in a rare interview with BBC Radio Leicester in October.

Khun Top, however, has now said that there were no takers when investment had been sought for a side that the Srivaddhanaprabha family, through its King Power duty free business in Thailand, have owned for 16 years.

"We recently undertook a structured process to explore whether new investment or a change of ownership could actually be the right thing for the club," Khun Top wrote in an open letter to Leicester City supporters on the club's website., external

"Those discussions have not resulted in an agreement, and I have decided to conclude the process to enable us to refocus on the work needed to move the club forward."

'Business as always' - Foxes boss Martin brushes off sales talk

Listen to BBC Radio Leicester's When You're Smiling podcast

Pre-match, post-match and topical Foxes content

Three relegations in four years, having yo-yoed between the Premier League and Championship before going down to League One, has badly damaged the relationship between the Foxes' owners and their supporter base.

While a golden age of success was bankrolled by King Power, with Premier League glory in 2016 followed up by FA Cup success in 2021, high spending on an underperforming side in recent years has led to an increasing number of supporters calling for Khun Top to sell up.

But the Thai businessman said he has a "deep connection" to Leicester and "its people".

And it is not just euphoric sporting moments that have forged the bond he is talking about, as his father - and predecessor as Foxes chairman - Khun Vichai died in a helicopter crash outside the stadium in 2018.

"For my family and me, Leicester City has been a big part of our lives for many years," he said.

"We have experienced extraordinary moments together, as well as some very difficult ones."

Khun Top added that the struggles of recent years, which included the club being hit with a points penalty last season for breaking spending rules, has got him "thinking a lot about our direction".

Earlier this year he told BBC Radio Leicester that he shoulders the blame for the club's decline.

"Making better decisions" as well as "continuing to learn from our past experiences" are two steps the club "need to take", he said.

Khun Top has insisted that through King Power, a company that has endured difficulties in recent years, the club's "financial position remains secure".

However, he added that there was "work needed to put Leicester City on a more sustainable footing".

"That has been a principle behind the work and decisions of the last year â giving the club the appropriate support for its immediate circumstances, while building the organisational discipline and financial resilience that will underpin a responsible plan for future growth," he said.

As part of Khun Top's missive, he confirmed that chief executive Kevin Davies will be stepping down from the role in December.

Davies had only been in the job since March, and was promoted to the position after a shake-up of a number of leadership roles.

#733. Watford appoint Iordanescu as head coach

Edward Iordanescu took Romania to the last 16 at Euro 2024

Watford have appointed former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu as the Championship club's new head coach.

The 48-year-old replaces Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge following a run of seven defeats in their past 10 league games, culminating in Saturday's 4-0 loss to Sheffield United.

"I am very proud and happy to be at this football club," Iordanescu told the club website., external

"I can see the team is in a difficult moment but I have already watched many of the games over the last few days and I'm very confident about the future."

He becomes Watford's sixth new boss in less than 18 months and is the 25th manager since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

Pioneer or coach-eater? The complex world of Pozzo's Watford

The former CFR Cluj and Legia Warsaw manager will be joined at Watford by backroom staff Alexandru Radu, Grzegorz Mokry and Michele Iannucci, but will watch Wednesday's Championship match at home to Blackburn Rovers from the stands before taking charge for Saturday's game at Derby.

Adrian Mariappa will oversee Wednesday's match at Vicarage Road (19:45 GMT), alongside Paul Furlong and Lloyd Doyley.

The Watford job is Iordanescu's first since leaving Legia Warsaw in October 2025, where he won the Super Cup last season.

It is the 10th managerial post of his 15-year coaching career, which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj - who he guided to the Romanian title and two domestic cups after joining midway through the 2020-21 season.

He also spent two-and-a-half years in charge of Romania, guiding them to the last 16 of Euro 2024, where they were beaten by the Netherlands.

Iordanescu takes over a Watford side currently three points above the relegation zone, having won only four of their 16 games so far.

Watford will be Iordanescu's first job in English football

Although untried in English football, Watford are getting a trophy-winning head coach with a wide-ranging CV spanning spells in his homeland, Bulgaria and Poland, as well as elite-level international experience with Romania.

His connections with his national side run deep as the son of his country's legendary former head coach Anghel Iordanescu, who famously took them to the quarter-finals of the 1994 World Cup during a reign of more than 100 games.

It is likely he will need every bit of that nous and inspiration as he becomes the latest boss to try to revive a club which continues to plough through managers at an alarming rate.

Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, with Iordanescu becoming the sixth permanent boss since Tom Cleverley was sacked in May 2025.

The Hornets' slow start to the season - with only four home wins and one point out of 24 away - has played out against the backdrop of uncertainty and unrest off the pitch.

Watford's owner, Gino Pozzo, is currently standing trial in Spain as one of a number of defendants accused of tax offences relating to Spanish team Granada, a club he used to be associated with.

He denies the allegations, which are related to player trading at Granada.

The case continues a tumultuous period for the club, with supporter and former owner Elton John voicing his frustration after a 4-0 home defeat by Burnley last month.

Fans have also questioned the running of the club, with one supporters' group declaring a loss of confidence in the ownership.

Iordanescu's immediate concern will be improving results, particularly Watford's form on the road, where they have yet to win and have conceded 18 goals in eight matches - with only Burnley letting in more.

He arrives with a reputation for defensive organisation and stability, of which the Hornets are in desperate need.

Geoff Doyle, BBC Three Counties Radio sports editor

So Watford try again with a new head coach - it is a regular occurrence at Vicarage Road.

Iordanescu has a decent CV with his work overseas in Romania, Bulgaria and Poland and is well thought of as a coach and manager.

But a lack of Championship experience is a concern and he is thrown in at the deep end with his new team hovering just above the relegation zone and confidence and morale low.

Iordanescu needs to hit the ground running in a critical week with the Hornets up against mid-table Blackburn and then Derby who are in the relegation zone.

#731. Violet Witchel Won’t Judge You for These Thanksgiving Dinner Shortcuts

Thanksgiving is practically here, and we turned to content creator and cookbook author Violet Witchel for some last-minute hosting tips, dinner shortcuts and more.

While we're getting ready to shop until we drop on Black Friday, let's not forget about what comes first: Thanksgiving. The holiday that's all about food and family can also come with a side of stress, especially if you're hosting.

We chatted exclusively with Violet Witchel, content creator and cookbook author, whose dense bean salads have totally transformed how I think about meal prepping for the week. And she came through with the best tips to help us with hosting, prepping food and even being a great holiday guest!

But if you're feeling stressed about your Thanksgiving menu and how you can get all the cooking and prep work done in time for dinner... don't be! Because guess what, even chefs like Violet pick up a few pre-made ingredients to help save time.

"Pre-made pie crust, mixes - like if you're going to make cornbread, get cornbread mix. Canned cranberry sauce, totally fine," she said of the items she'd get from the store. "Pre-bought stuffing, like the mix, totally fine. Pre-minced vegetables, totally fine."

But one thing you won't catch her using? Powdered mashed potatoes. "I think on Thanksgiving, you've gotta do that from scratch."

And whether you're team pumpkin, apple or pecan, supporting a local bakery is not only tasty but also a time-saver she added. Don't forget the canned whipped cream and your favorite ice cream!

For more food prep advice and tips from Violet, keep reading!

"I don't love to bring wine because I feel like everyone brings wine and they feel kind of obligated to serve it at dinner," Violet shared. "So I love to bring a nice bottle of olive oil because it's one of those things you're like 'oh, this is wonderful to have.' "

This duo by Brightland is on sale and ready for gifting! It includes the smooth and delicate Alive EVOO, the bold and robust Awake EVOO, two gold pouring spouts, and comes gift-ready in a 2026 holiday box.

These lush pink and green leaves, available in a pot color of your choosing, on this Aglaonema cultivar, will thrive in a variety of light levels.

And for the person in your life that is always cooking, they should definitely have fresh herbs at home if they don't already. "I love basil, especially if you have a sunny window. I feel like basil can withstand anything," she shared.

Grow your own herbs at home! This kit comes with three basil pods and a grow light if you don't have a sunny window.

"You might not think a candle in the bathroom is a hosting essential, but it is," Violet said. "I love the Flamingo Estate candles. I think they're so chic, they burn forever, they smell so good. I love them."

Violet loves the "summery and earthy" scent of Flamingo Estate's Heirloom Tomato candle, which she says can go into fall or winter.

"An immersion blender is kind of my holy grail, I use that for everything. Pulling out a full food processor or blender is kind of an ordeal, but if you want to make a delicious, perfectly blended dressing, an immersion blender is so perfect for that."

#730. Lincoln sack head coach duo Cohen and Shaw after only six months

Chris Cohen (left) and Tom Shaw had been on the coaching staff together at Lincoln for a number of years before they got the top job together

Lincoln City have sacked their head coaches Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw just six months after they took joint charge of the Championship side.

The pair departed a little over 12 hours after they oversaw a 4-0 defeat at fellow strugglers Charlton Athletic on Tuesday.

The loss leaves the Imps just three points above the relegation places in what is the club's first season back in the second tier for 65 years.

Cohen and Shaw were assistant coaches under Michael Skubala when Lincoln were promoted as League One title winners last season.

They were surprisingly promoted to replace their boss as a managerial double act.

Championship survival behind sackings - Imps CEO

What next for Lincoln City after coach duo exit?

The duo oversaw just four wins from 17 league games this season, and Tuesday's loss at The Valley was their fifth in succession and heaviest since being thumped 6-0 by West Ham in mid-October.

Lincoln's chairman Ron Fowler, the American billionaire who took a controlling stake in the club when they were on their way to promotion last season, said the decision to sack the pair was in the "best interests" of the Imps.

"We have worked incredibly hard to reach the Championship and will do everything in our power to retain our status in this division," he told the club website., external

First-team coach Shaun Pearson will take charge of Lincoln, with the support of Paul McShane and David Preece, on an interim basis.

Lincoln are next in action on Saturday when they host high-flying Wolves.

When Cohen and Shaw got the job at Sincil Bank it came somewhat as a shock because managing football teams in tandem is somewhat of a curiosity in the game.

Liverpool famously did with Gerard Houllier and Roy Evans in 1998 when the partnership lasted six months as results slumped, while Tottenham gave it a go with Doug Livermore and Ray Clemence earlier that same decade.

The hope was that the Cohen-Shaw show would be a lot more like Coventry's success story under John Sillett and George Curtis, who guided the Sky Blues to FA Cup glory in 1987.

Lincoln's decision-makers were proactive in talking up their decision, with sporting director Jez George explaining in June that the appointment "wasn't a case of do the easy thing, but it was absolutely the right thing for the club".

Shaw and Cohen were also quizzed at length about how the joint role would work, starting with "who's going to make the subs?"

Cohen was upfront when he said "from the outside looking in, it's not normal", but the former Nottingham Forest and West Ham midfielder insisted that the job share was "really normal" to them.

How peculiar it might have looked, or how the dynamics between the pair worked, all become somewhat irrelevant in recent weeks as Lincoln's dire run of form has plunged them towards the relegation places.

Pre-match, post-match and topical Imps content

Lincoln City fans always thought this season would be tough and that they'd lose more than they win, but it was the manner of the performances recently that was most concerning.

Strange team selections in the past two matches in particular, including playing left-back Adam Reach as a right winger against Charlton Athletic in their final match in charge, was always going to raise questions, especially when the results didn't go their way, and that has ultimately been the case.

The appointment of Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw was going to be seen as a risk - joint managers/head coaches very rarely work and add in the lack of managerial experience, especially at this level.

First-team coach Shaun Pearson, who only recently joined the club , now has the task to try to turn a team low on confidence, low on ideas and low on belief into one that can stop one of the promotion favourites in Wolves on Saturday lunchtime.

Whoever's next in the dugout, however, won't come in with a massive jump in expectations of a climb up the table.

Imps supporters will be more than happy to just see their side secure a second season in the Championship.

#729. How to unearth young stars, the Bayern Munich way

Bayern initially aim to find young players from Bavaria before looking further afield

Bayern Munich are one of the elite powers in European football and current home of Ballon d'Or winner and England captain Harry Kane.

But, while Kane is the latest hugely successful foreign import at Bayern, the German giants also put a particular focus on producing their own elite young talent.

In 2013, Bayern had four homegrown players in the starting line-up as they won the Champions League.

Repeating that victory, and continuing the club's history of nurturing young players, is what director of youth development and campus Jochen Sauer says Bayern are aiming for.

Sauer joined from Red Bull Salzburg in 2017 when the academy campus opened in another part of Munich, away from the first-team training complex.

The club's motto "Mia San Mia" translates to "we are who we are" and Sauer says it has always been the club's goal to have a local homegrown element in its senior side.

"It was always our identity and philosophy to be a regional club, but at the same time to be competitive internationally and on Champions League level," Sauer tells BBC Sport.

"But always having a core of our team coming from the Munich area and the Bavarian region with a deep identification with the club and the city.

"Our recruitment guidelines, especially for the under-11 to the under-15 teams, is trying to recruit as much talent as possible from the Munich area and the region of Bavaria."

Munich-born Croatia international Josip Stanisic is a good example. The midfielder, 26, signed as an under-17 player from local outfit SC Furstenfeldbruck, while 22-year-old Aleksandar Pavlovic joined the academy aged eight and has worked his way up to the first team and is a Germany international.

But perhaps the biggest name to come out of the academy in recent times is Jamal Musiala. The former Chelsea youth player, who joined aged 16, is a star for Bayern and Germany and has already won six Bundesliga titles at just 23 years old.

It was part of the club's strategy to bring in the best young foreign players, and those with German passports, to the club, but they also enjoyed a bit of luck.

The move came around the time Bayern Munich were interested in then-Chelsea winger Callum Hudson-Odoi, who shared the same agent as Musiala, who moved from Germany to England when he was seven.

Bayern were already aware of Musiala because he was born in Germany, but the timing was right to make a deal happen.

"There were for sure some pieces that came together at that time," Sauer says.

"I think one reason why we fought for the player at that time was the reason we had the feeling that Chelsea is not really seeing his full potential to be a top player for their first team.

"Because, otherwise, if they would have seen him as a future prospect, then it would been hard, even for Bayern Munich, to get a player out of the Chelsea environment."

Other young players in the first-team squad include 18-year-old Bara Sapoko Ndiaye, signed from Gambinos Stars Africa in The Gambia, and 18-year-old Lennart Karl, who joined the academy four years ago and has been capped by Germany.

Shirts with Bayern's academy graduates adorn the walls of their youth campus

The Bayern Campus can house up to 43 players in accommodation, predominantly local players before they widen the search overseas.

"I think there is basically kind of a guideline that we want to have a minimum 60% of the players coming from the region and reaching the level of the under-19 age group," Sauer says.

"This automatically means that the other 40% of the team has to be recruited from other regions nationwide.

"Coming to an age group of under-17, we are also reaching out to the main European football markets to recruit the most talented players internationally.

"Jamal Musiala is one perfect example. As soon as we're coming to an age of 16 and the regulations allow us to do international transfers, we want to recruit the best talents in Europe. That's for sure part of our recruitment philosophy."

Another piece that fell into place for Musiala was the Bayern under-17 team at that time was coached by Miroslav Klose, the former Bayern forward who is the record goalscorer for Germany.

Klose is credited with pushing Musiala to work on the defensive side of his game. He also knew what a player needed to get to the highest level, with the former striker becoming an assistant to Hansi Flick when Musiala joined the first team.

That idea of having former players in charge of the next generation continues.

Ex-Bayern centre-back Dante, who also played for Nice for more than 10 years, is the current under-19 head coach.

"They can inject a little bit of the Bayern Munich DNA into the players," Sauer explains. "More from a personality side, not necessarily from a playing style.

"He also has some different ideas on the playing style but you know playing for Bayern Munich and being in the first team of Bayern Munich, at least they can tell our players what they have to be from a character, from a personality to make it up to the first team."

With so many players coming into the system and a difficult first-team set-up to break into, the Bayern style remains consistent throughout age groups.

Coaches are given guidelines to work towards but it does not stop them from having their own ideas as they aim for a style of "dominance and intensity".

"But football is always a process of evaluation," Sauer says.

"Opening the campus in 2017, we have put a very clear idea of football in place, but always kept the openness to add in ideas from coaches like [Jupp] Heynckes, [Julian] Nagelsmann, [Thomas] Tuchel, Hansi Flick, and, for sure, [current Bayern manager Vincent] Kompany. The football is always developing.

"So we have to be open enough always to amend little things. But I would say that the overall strategy is still what it was in the times of Heynckes, Pep Guardiola or Louis van Gaal."

There is an eye-catching display in one of the well-kept corridors of Bayern's campus. Shirts of high-profile academy graduates are framed on the walls, with a display showing tiers of Germany's football leagues and players who have played in them.

To qualify for the display, players need to have played a minimum of 30 full 90-minute games.

Bayern say that almost 44% of the young players who are in their youth set-up until the under-19 team become a professional player.

"The success is not only bringing players to Allianz Arena, but bringing players also to professional football. This is also essential if you want to convince a young talented player to be part of Bayern Munich," Sauer adds.

"For us, it's more the story: Listen, if you're coming to Bayern Munich we cannot guarantee that you will be a first-team player at Bayern Munich, because it's very tough to achieve. And you have a lot of world-class players around you. So if you are a top striker and you have Harry Kane there it will be difficult to replace him.

"But what we can at least guarantee you is we can teach you and develop you to a level that you have a very, very big chance to be a professional football player at least in a tier one, tier two or tier-three club."

Like most things in modern football, the development of players also has to make business sense for the six-time European champions, who last won the Champions League in 2019-20.

"Being in a competition with Paris St-Germain, all the English and the Spanish clubs to win the Champions League, it would be almost unrealistic to say we want to have 11 players on the pitch that play for our academy," says Sauer.

"But I think if we can reach the goal that we always have five or six players steadily in the first team, that would be a great success.

"On the other side, and this is more I would say economical answer, we do not have the money of the English clubs. We do not have the TV money. To be still competitive over the next decade, I think we all also have to make money with our players."

Examples over the past two years include selling forward Mathys Tel to Tottenham, left-back Adam Aznou to Everton, midfielder Paul Wanner to PSV and striker Jonah Kusi-Asare to Fulham.

"So I would say [our] final goal would be to develop every year a player from our academy to the first team and probably sell some others for a significant amount.

"[That] would be something that is a combination that would help us on the one side to have a good and competitive Bayern Munich team and on the other side to be still competitive on a level with Man City, Liverpool, Madrid and Barcelona.

"So I think that's those two goals that we have, bring players to Allianz Arena and make money."

#728. Raheem Sterling - from national icon to suspended jail sentence

Raheem Sterling has scored 123 goals in 396 Premier League appearances and provided 65 assists

Raheem Sterling grew up a stone's throw from Wembley Stadium, and went on to start a European Championship final for England there.

At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning Â£325,000 a week at Chelsea.

"Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," said then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a Â£50m deal in 2022.

"He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example.

"He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us."

Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal, and commanded combined transfer fees of about Â£100m.

But his career at the top level looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.

At an earlier hearing in September, Sterling admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before crashing a Lamborghini on 28 May.

The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

Sterling also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

How Sterling went from England star to court appearance

Sterling's life was touched by tragedy at a young age.

Born in Kingston, Jamaica, he was just two when his father was shot dead.

His mother, Nadine, was determined to give her children a safer environment to live in. She moved to England to lay a path for Sterling and his sister to join her once she had found a home and finished her education, while cleaning bathrooms and changing bedsheets in hotels to earn extra money.

Sterling grew up on a housing estate in Neasden, north-west London, and spent part of his education at Vernon House, where teachers attempted to help the football-obsessed youngster with behavioural problems.

In an interview with the Players' Tribune, external in 2018, Sterling said: "I was so naughty that they kicked me out of primary school. I just didn't like to listen to anyone but my mum. That was my problem."

He was 10 when teacher Chris Beschi told him: "If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or in prison."

Sterling would grow to become one of the standout English attacking talents of his generation.

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

Raheem Sterling: From school struggles to a class of his own

On 14 November 2012 - aged 17 years and 342 days - Sterling made his England debut on the night his Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard won his 100th cap in a 4-2 defeat by Sweden in Stockholm.

Sterling would go on to make 81 more appearances for his country, scoring 20 goals.

He featured at three World Cups - 2014, 2018 and 2022 - and two European Championships. He was one of the standout players as England reached the Euro 2020 final at Wembley, where they were beaten by Italy.

Sterling was now at the peak of his career - the former Queens Park Rangers youngster, who has a tattoo on his forearm of a young boy holding a football looking up at the Wembley arch, named in the team of the tournament by Uefa.

Liverpool had signed a 15-year-old Sterling from QPR for Â£600,000 in February 2010.

He made his senior Reds debut two years later and became the second-youngest goalscorer in their history - behind Michael Owen - when he scored the winner against Reading in October 2012 at the age of 17.

In 2015, Sterling joined Manchester City in a deal worth up to Â£49m, making him the most expensive English player at the time.

He had been under contract at Anfield until 2017 but turned down a new deal to move to Liverpool's rivals, with City boss Manuel Pellegrini describing the 20-year-old as "one of the best attacking players in world football".

Sterling went on to score 131 goals in 339 appearances in all competitions during seven successful years at Etihad Stadium.

As well as four Premier League titles, he helped City win five League Cups, one FA Cup and one Community Shield.

It was while he was at City, in 2021, that Sterling became an MBE in the Queen's Birthday Honours for his services to racial equality in sport.

"I am grateful to have been recognised," he said. "But my priority is to try to help to educate society and myself. I'm learning every day."

After City came the move to Chelsea, where his career began to stall.

Tuchel, now England manager, was sacked two months after signing Sterling, who made just 45 Premier League starts for the Blues over four years.

Off the pitch, he launched a scholarship fund aimed at closing the gap in the number of black British students who go to university.

On the pitch, he was finding it a struggle.

He spent 18 months as a member of Chelsea's so-called 'bomb squad', and a season-long loan to Arsenal in 2024-25 proved largely unsuccessful.

Sterling: If you grew up in a certain area you feel like there's limits

As well as his success on the field, Sterling has made headlines off it too.

In 2015, when he was 20, reports began to surface about his behaviour away from the game.

Sterling was pictured apparently inhaling nitrous oxide and was also photographed smoking a shisha pipe.

That prompted then Liverpool boss Brendan Rodgers to warn Sterling he would "look back in 20 years and wonder what he was doing".

Sterling also made headlines while on duty for England at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

The Sun ran a story titled "Raheem shoots himself in the foot" as pictures emerged of a tattoo of an M16 assault rifle on his leg.

Sterling explained on social media: "When I was 2 my father died from being gunned down to death I made a promise to myself I would never touch a gun in my life time. I shoot with my right foot so it has a deeper meaning."

The incident led to a widespread discussion in the UK about the treatment of black athletes in the media, with comparisons drawn between how Sterling's life was covered compared to others.

Sterling spoke out a number of times on the issue and wider racism in society, which was reflected in him being made an MBE.

Five years after his MBE, Sterling's career has stalled. He has not played since appearing for Feyenoord on 17 May, after agreeing a short-term move to the Netherlands.

Eleven days after that game, he was arrested after crashing a Lamborghini near the M3 in Hampshire.

Watch: Sterling joins PL 100 club - best goals & stats

Listen: From Wembley schoolboy to playing for England at Wembley

Sterling was riding the crest of a wave when he moved from Manchester City to Chelsea in the summer of 2022 for Â£50m.

His medal cabinet was already fit to burst with 10 major trophies under Guardiola and, alongside Harry Kane, he was arguably England's most important player for then head coach Gareth Southgate.

Tuchel viewed Sterling as his number one target that summer and Chelsea's new ownership - Behdad Eghbali and Todd Boehly - delivered as the club entered the post-Roman Abramovich era.

Two months later, Tuchel was sacked and Graham Potter was in situ.

Sterling's career has not been the same since.

It is, of course, senseless to suggest the troubles Sterling has had on and off the pitch in recent years are simply down to the sacking of Tuchel in 2022.

But speak to those close to Sterling and they will explain Tuchel was among the key factors behind the winger's decision to swap Manchester for west London.

He was captivated by Tuchel's vision, not only for the team, but his role in it.

#727. Rylee Arnold's Boyfriend Posts Message on DWTS Finale With Connor Wood

Dancing With the Stars pro Rylee Arnold—partnered with influencer Connor Wood—shared how her boyfriend, Walker Lyons, supported their team ahead of the season 35 finale.

Rylee Arnold's boyfriend thinks Connor Wood is all that jazz.

After Wood addressed fans who hoped that his partnership with his Dancing With the Stars coach might translate off the dance floor, the pro's real-life match, BYU football player Walker Lyons, chimed in with support for the team taking home the season 35 title.

"Today is the day! So proud of you and the work you have put in to get here, so deserving," Lyons captioned a shot of Arnold holding a supersized bouquet of roses on Instagram Stories Nov. 24. As for the influencer known as Fibula, he added, "Vote for Connor."

And the 21-year-old treasured the romantic gesture from her boyfriend of two years, calling the floral display that arrived that morning, "the best surprise ever."

Wood, 31, previously tap-danced past speculation about his relationship with Arnold in a Nov. 10 TikTok Live, sharing one message for viewers wishing to turn his shot at the Mirrorball into fan fiction: "I say, 'Thank you for watching.'"

However, Arnold had plenty of words to express how much she valued finding a romance with Lyons.

"There were so many crazy coincidences that actually brought us together," she told E! News following the Halloween episode Oct. 30. "He’s just such a great guy, I really found a good one who makes me feel so special. And we have so much fun together."

The Dancing with the Stars: Juniors alum added regarding the attention around her onscreen chemistry with Wood that she told the 22-year-old, "'It's scary I know,'" noting how Lyons has been "the best sport about it—he’s just the best."

As such, Arnold didn't hold back when remarking how excited she was to find a platonic partner in crime in the podcaster for her fourth season as a pro.

"It just feels natural," Arnold told Entertainment Weekly in September. "I think naturally we just have so much fun together. We feel comfortable with each other."

But that doesn't mean all of the dancing duos on the ABC competition series stayed just pals. For more stars and pros who foxtrotted out of friendship on DWTS, keep reading...

The season 33 partners dated for about seven months between 2024 and spring 2025.

In April 2025, the fellow DWTS pros kissed on the lips onstage on the final night of the series' 2025 tour during their show-closing duet dance, confirming months of romance rumors.

Months after placing fifth in the 31st season of the dance show, the couple confirmed their romance on Valentine's Day 2023. "My Valentine," the CODA actor captioned a selfie with the choreographer. "Happy Valentine's Day!"

Stewart and Durant then announced their engagement in December 2023 and married in front of a trouple of DWTS pros in August 2025.

While she was partnered with Hayes Grier, the two hit it off during season 21's Switch Up Week, with Skarlatos calling the pro dancer "so hot." After her elimination, Slater teased that they two had yet to go on a date, saying, "We'll see."

Meanwhile, Skarlatos playfully told E! News, "No comment!"

The dance pro and Bachelorette alum were romantically linked while competing together on DWTS' season 33 in 2024. However, their offscreen chemistry fizzled out by June 2025 shortly after Tran returned to Miami to finish her master's degree.

Which bring us to these two. After dating a little on-and-off since 2011, the pros got engaged live on the show in October 2016 and were married in March 2018. However, E! News confirmed in August 2022 that Slater and Farber were going their separate ways after four years of marriage.

"It's not a nightmare at all," Slater told E! News. "We support each other so much that I want the very best for Sasha. We support each other, very, very truly."

Chmerkovskiy and Johnson were dating in 2015, before she was promoted to pro dancer. They got engaged in June of 2018 before making it official and walking down the aisle in April of 2019. The two welcomed son Rome Valentin in January 2023.

"Life is awesome," Chmerkovskiy told E! News in May 2023. Becoming a dad "definitely elevated my joy for life, my joy for my family, and every day I learn something new being a father."

In December 2020, E! News learned the Selling Sunset star was dating the Dancing With the Stars pro after they had competed separately on season 29.

However, after two months of dating, E! News exclusively confirmed they had called it quits. At the time, a source close to the realtor said, "They had a fun time together but in the end, decided it would be best if they part ways. They are still friendly and cordial. It wasn't a messy breakup, just wasn't the right fit or right timing."

Platonic throughout their seventh-place-finishing 2017 run, the Total Bellas star and the former Dancing With the Stars pro found their way back to each other after her split from John Cena in 2018. Garcia confirmed her relationship with Chigvintsev in May 2019, and they got engaged later that year.

The WWE Hall of Famer learned she was expecting soon after their Paris engagement, with them welcoming son Matteo Artemovich Chigvintsev in 2020.

Sadly, though, the pair are no longer partnering up. Garcia filed for divorce in September 2024, two weeks after Chigvintsev was arrested on suspicion of domestic violence. Ultimately, the Napa County District Attorney's office announced they decided not to file charges against him "after a thorough review of the criminal investigation and careful evaluation of the evidence presented to the DA’s Office."

The pair settled their divorce in November 2024, with Garcia's rep noting the two also dropped their "the domestic violence restraining orders against each other in an effort to move on with their lives and effectively co-parent their son."

The model and the relatively new pro flirted up a storm throughout season 27, and Ren had admitted on the show that she had a crush on him. At the time, a source even told E! News that they "really enjoy each other's company" and were "seeing where things go."

However, multiple outlets reported in December 2018 that the pair had split.

The professional dancers got engaged on Dec. 5, 2015, after dating since 2012. Maks proposed onstage at the SWAY: A Dance Trilogy event in Miami. Six months after welcoming their son Shai, the lovebirds exchanged vows during a lavish ceremony in July 2017. They then welcomed baby Rio in June 2023 and their third son Milan in July 2024.

The partners struck up a romance in season five, but broke up a few months after their shocking exit. Still, Bryan and Ballas remained friendly, with The Cheetah Girls star even returning to the ballroom to cheer for him the following season.

Funnily enough, the duo had gone out on several dates before he even signed up for the show. And while they denied any romance rumors during season 18, that didn't stop them from playing up their chemistry during performances.

Soon after the Shark Tank star announced he was separating from his wife of 14 years Diane Plese, sources confirmed to E! News that he and Kym Johnson, his pro partner from season 20, were dating and "really happy together."

While Robert and Kym at first played coy about the nature of their relationship, that quickly stopped. They were engaged in February 2016, married by June 2016, and welcomed twins in April 2018.

Partnered in season three, the Saved by the Bell alum quickly struck up a romance with the dance pro, which went on for two years before they called it off for good in 2008. "The relationship wasn't heading in the right direction," Smirnoff's rep said in a statement, after rumors of infidelity on Lopez's part.

The professional dancers got engaged in 2009 after six months of dating following her split from Mario Lopez. Sadly, they called it off later that same year. But the duo remained friendly, even going on vacations together.

Married since 2014, the pros announced the arrival of their daughter Nikita in May 2023.

Daniella shared the happy news by posting a photo and video of Pasha with Nikita to Instagram Stories. She wrote "daddy's girl" alongside the clip and "My Geminis" beside the picture.

After showing off their insane chemistry during the sixth season, the duo dated for nearly a year before announcing their 2009 breakup in the most cordial way ever: matching tweets! "Hi everyone, we wanted you all to know directly from us, that Shannon & I have decided to end our relationship as boyfriend & girlfriend...," Hough tweeted that August, with Elizabeth writing, "However, we love and care about each other very much and will remain friends and in each others lives."

Derek is now married to his dance partner Hayley Erbert.

#726. COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels

The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."

Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.

"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.

"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.

Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.

"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."

"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.

"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.

"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."

But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."

David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.

"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."

Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.

#725. Confusion and anger - Yoro red card rescinded, but row goes on

Leny Yoro will be available for Manchester United's game against Brentford on Saturday after his one-match ban was rescinded

Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.

Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.

Referee Sam Barrott sent off the France international, and the decision was backed up by video assistant referee (VAR) John Brooks.

It split opinion among pundits and fans. Would Isak have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens? Was it really a clear goalscoring chance?

First, a Football Association regulatory commission upheld United's appeal and cancelled the red card.

Then Pro Ref boss Howard Webb said the red card was not "clearly wrong" - just moments before United held a pre-match news conference.

Over to Red Devils head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was fiercely critical of the decision, and in particular the VAR.

But how can Pro Ref still believe the decision was right when an FA commission said it was wrong?

So United won their appeal. Pro Ref would disagree. Could the two sides not just agree to differ?

"You ask me a question and I need to defend our situation and our club and our players," Pochettino said about Yoro's red card.

It continued a theme from his post-match news conference.

You can see why Pochettino would be keen to talk about the red card, rather than the performance of his players. After all, United had just lost the first game of his tenure. Was the Argentine keen to create a siege mentality?

You can also understand United's frustration - two of their biggest games of the season so far have been defined by refereeing decisions.

The first was the VAR error to allow Erling Haaland's match-winning goal in the Manchester derby, when Enzo Fernandez clearly committed an offside offence.

As for the Yoro incident, Pochettino reserved much his criticism for the VAR. United felt he only took a cursory look at where the ball would run.

It should be noted that Match Officials Mic'd up, on which Webb gave his views, was filmed on Monday evening - before the result of the appeal.

Would that change his opinion? Almost certainly not.

Webb acknowledged the argument against a red card, which was Isak would not get the ball. But he was adamant it was not such an egregious error that it required a VAR intervention.

So are we back to arguing about when VAR should get involved?

The VAR threshold is too high, until it is too low. Rinse and repeat.

It is the Premier League clubs, and not Pro Ref nor the FA, who set where the bar sits.

Take the last stakeholders' survey, which helps to shape how the game is officiated.

It found 65% wanted to maintain the current threshold for VAR intervention, 20% to increase it, and just 15% to lower it.

But, of course, where the Yoro incident sits is still a matter of opinion.

'And the three points?' - Pochettino after Yoro red overturned

How confusing it must be for a supporter just watching on, hoping to understand.

An FA regulatory commission has said the red card decision was wrong. Case closed? Not so fast.

Pro Ref will not always agree with the decision of an appeal board, nor will they use it as a barometer for future decisions.

And the burden of proof for a VAR intervention is considered higher than for an FA commission.

Pro Ref places far more stock upon the judgements of the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.

The KMI Panel creates the merit table for referees, and helps shape how decisions are made in the future - especially for the VARs.

But surely the FA is the higher body? Not quite.

The FA is responsible purely for disciplinary measures and has no say on how games at the professional level are refereed.

If the Premier League tells Pro Ref the decision is right or wrong, that counts far more than any vote by an FA commission.

BBC Sport understands the club argued that if Isak had maintained his top recorded speed, he would not have got to the ball first.

The club say that is objectively provable, within minutes, using data. This, they say, was not a subjective decision.

To argue it was not subjective goes completely against the nature of the decision - it required a referee's judgement.

Whatever this data was, it most definitely was not available to the referees. The VAR cannot call upon a 3D animation of each player, detailing their running speed and providing an objective result.

How much stock did the commission place on this evidence? We will not know until the written reasons are published in a few days' time.

But United are not going to let this lie, and Pro Ref is not going to bend.

Such is the way FA commissions work, you can never be sure who will win.

There are three panel members who are usually former players, but occasionally you might get a retired referee.

The role of the commission is not to "usurp the referee by re-refereeing the incident".

A designated referee delegate is present to answer questions on the laws of the game, but they cannot offer an opinion on the incident.

The only input Pro Ref has is the official's report - a short entry by the referee that says which law was used for the red card. There is no other context.

It will read something like this: "I have to report that I, as the referee, sent off Yoro, Leny of Manchester United FC Under Law 12 section: S5."

The burden is on the club to prove its case by submitting a body of evidence - videos, images and testimony.

There is no right of reply. The evidence is weighed up by the panel, a vote is cast and the majority wins.

It makes predicting the outcome notoriously difficult, as the system is an opinion poll based upon a club trying to persuade at least two people to agree with them.

Take a look at Aston Villa's successful appeal against Douglas Luiz's red card for violent conduct four years ago. Luiz had been sent off via a VAR review for a headbutt on Aleksandar Mitrovic.

The panel's written reasons stated the appeal was won partly because Luiz was "a few inches shorter than Mr Mitrovic so his forehead is naturally at the same height as Mr Mitrovic's nose/face as the two players come together".

So, when the two players bumped chests the headbutt was just an accident. Appeal upheld because Luiz was a bit shorter.

Some might think anything is worth trying.

#724. Dancing With the Stars Season 35 Winner Revealed After Major Comeback

DWTS crowned Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach the champions of season 35 during the nail-biting Nov. 24 finale after out-dancing Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins, Tatyana Ali and Connor Wood.

Dancing With the Stars’ new champion sprinted straight to the top.

During the season 35 finale, Ezra Frech and partner Daniella Karagach secured the Mirrorball Trophy after making an incredible recovery from a prosthetic mishap during their freestyle—making Frech the first Paralympian to take home the title.

And it's clear the pair found their rhythm, delivering show-stopping routines during the Nov. 24 episode. In addition to receiving perfect scores by judges Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba and Bruno Tonioli, Ezra also becomes the first amputee to win the show and the youngest man to win at 21, besting last year's champ Robert Irwin.

"This is the most special moment of my life," Ezra shared. "Thank you, everybody, for voting. Thank you for believing in us. Oh my God."

Daniella—earning her second Mirrorball following her victory with Iman Shumpert in season 30—added, "I'm just so freaking grateful."

Of course, the 2026 champions achieving the sole purpose of the competition meant they outscored runner-up Amber Glenn, as well as Connor Wood, Tatyana Ali and Maura Higgins.

In a salsa danced to "Danza Kuduro," Ezra and Daniella set the stage on fire. To switch things up, the runner also landed an empowering freestyle to "Numb" by Linkin Park, which Daniella teased on the show's official podcast Nov. 19 would include moves that have "definitely never been done before," like Ezra beginning the routine without his prosthetic.

After putting on the device mid-routine, it unsuctioned later in the dance, but he was able to make an impressive recovery, with Derek raving, "The worst-case scenario might have happened and you wouldn't even have known, the way you rose in that moment."

Meanwhile, Amber and partner Pasha Pashkov moved their feet to a quickstep set to "Sing Sing Sing" by Louis Prima, complemented by a colorful freestyle to Madonna hits "Like a Prayer" and "Music."

Wood led pro Rylee Arnold in an emotional Viennese Waltz, in addition to a freestyle mashing up "Singin’ in the Rain" and Rihanna's "Umbrella." They were joined by Rylee's sister, Lindsay Arnold Cusick, for the routine after the former pro stepped away from the show in 2021.

Love Island's Higgins tangoed with Mark Ballas, then balancing out the spicy number with a jazzy rendition of "Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend" featuring Irish folk song selections as a nod to her heritage. And Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik delivered the night's third tango, as well as a jazzy freestyle to a Judy Garland song that was out of this world.

Amber, Ezra and Maura all received perfect scores of 90 while Connor and Tatyana received 82 points from the judges.

Still, all of the finalists were surrounded by support from their previously eliminated castmates taking one more spin around the ballroom. Their return reminded viewers of the year's shocking twists and turns that sent home top performers like Harry Shum Jr., Jenna Dewan and Taylor Hanson despite their consistently positive feedback from the judges' panel.

On the other foot, stars like Julia Stiles and Ciara Miller—whose claim to fame in the competition became their heartfelt connection with partners Ezra Sosa and Brandon Armstrong, respectively—delighted the audience by coming in all smiles following their emotional eliminations.

That said, while only one winner can take home the title, DWTS has changed the lives of many of its alums. Read on for more secrets about the ABC series.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#723. Glasner criticises Forest players yet to learn English

Nottingham Forest have suffered successive 2-0 defeats on the road to Brentford and Bournemouth

Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner says standards at the club were not good enough when he arrived, and has questioned why some of his squad cannot speak English after being in the country for a number of years.

Forest are one place above the relegation zone heading into Friday's home game against Chelsea, winning just two of their first 11 games in the Premier League.

"Stability in a company is having standards," said Glasner. "Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough.

"We have players who are here for four years, can't speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language.

"For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English. If I want to manage in Italy, I have to speak Italian.

"Otherwise, Oliver Glasner, if you want to speak in your dialect, stay at home in Austria, everybody understands you, but nowhere else."

Forest, who narrowly avoided relegation last season but who did reach the Europa League semi-finals, have had a succession of managers in recent years and while Glasner refused to blame the upheaval for any problems he has inherited, he feels standards need to rise.

"We want to create a stable Nottingham Forest team that can consistently play in the top half of the Premier League," added Glasner, 52.

"We are a few steps away from this but we really believe we know which steps we have to take.

"We are still very ambitious but it looks to take a little bit longer than we all hoped. The goal is getting stability into this club and we're still working on this.

"We knew this is a transition season, let's say like this, where we still stay very ambitious but with a lot of problems to solve."

Glasner held transfer talks with Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis in London on Monday as the club prepares their plans for the January transfer window, when they hope to add up to five players to their squad.

"He [Marinakis] was asking 'what do you need, what do you want here to improve in the squad, the staff and the environment'," said Glasner.

"He wants the best for Nottingham Forest, he wants the best for everyone here.

"We need to improve in the squad, in the staff, in the environment and this is our discussion. It was a fantastic meeting and it was worth spending six hours travelling."
